speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion under Standing Order 43. Nearly four months ago my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), and I were denied unanimous consent for a motion which would have protested against the severe punishment imposed upon Bishop Lamont by Rhodesian authorities. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. I begin by welcoming the right hon. gentleman back to the House of Commons and extending to him the congratulations of this side of the House, and I am sure of all our colleagues, on the very effective speech that he delivered to the joint meeting of Congress.

Accommodations will be made, revisions will take place.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, in his response, referred to a variety of potential accommodations that might be made-I think I am quoting him correctly-to the province of Quebec and to the French fact. Is it his view that the only accommodations that are required to be made, the only major revisions that are required to be made in the interest of national unity of the country, relate to Quebec, relate to language and relate to the acceptance of the French fact? We are trying to get some understanding of the perspective with which he views his responsibilities as the leader of the national government.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PRIME MINISTER S REFERENCE TO REVISIONS AND ACCOMMODATIONS FOR QUEBEC
speechtext: The answer is, obviously not. The series of proposals we made, and to which I just referred, between 1968 and 1971 were addressed to all the provinces. They had to do with the sharing or division of powers which would be offered equally to every one of the provinces. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, I have always opposed, and I continue to oppose, any concept of a special status for any one province. But in the case of Quebec's feelings now, my whole argument is that the rest of Canada must accommodate to and accept the French fact, much as Qtiebecers must accept the Canadian reality and not try to solve the problems by separating.

Could the Prime Minister give a fuller explanation to the House of the yes and no answer given yesterday in response to a question. I think 1 have the question correct when I quote it in this way:
Canada-U.S. relations is the foundation stone of our foreign policy and consequently, whether that heralds the end of a more broadly based third option in foreign policy . . .

speechtext:

contemplated to condemn the violations of human rights which occur.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND PRESIDENT CARTER OF VIOLATIONS OF HELSINKI AGREEMENT-POSSIBILITY OF JOINT ACTION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, that question was discussed at some length, and the House well knows President Carter's interest in pursuing this objective of the respect of human rights. I repeat that we discussed it at some length, and we agreed that there should be continued co-operation between our two governments in preparation for the review of the Helsinki Pact which will be held in Belgrade, probably in the fall of this year. We agreed to make available to the United States information we have which relates particularly to the subject matters contained in the Third Basket, the reunification of families and the free flow of ideas, and President Carter indicated his interest in getting that information from us.

Will the Prime Minister take the opportunity at a suitable time to make a full statement to this House and detail changes, the accommodations and the revisions of the constitution to which he was referring in his address to the Congress of the United States?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CHANGES TO WHICH PRIME MINISTER REFERRED IN ADDRESS TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS-POSSIBILITY OF DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member also for his kind words regarding the honour I believe we all shared as parliamentarians, in being invited to address the Congress.
My answer to the hon. member's question would be quite a lengthy one and suggest a statement. I would attempt now to perhaps indicate the sense of any possible statement or action.
At the Victoria conference and in the correspondence to which I have just alluded in answering the Leader of the Opposition, we have already indicated several measures which in our view if introduced and guaranteed in the constitution, would constitute an entrenchment of the French fact in our constitution and give ample protection to some of the concerns that Quebecers express-the fear that they would not be protected permanently within the framework of our constitution. So, a lot is already on record as being part of the government's policy.
Beyond that, I would hesitate to undertake in any future statement to put before the House or before the Canadian public a whole series of amendments to the constitution just so that they be on the table for the provinces to reject or negotiate. I believe there has to be a will on the part of the provinces as well as the federal government to proceed with certain types of revision. We have certain ideas, to many of which I have just alluded to improve the constitution but I do not think it practicable to take initiatives which the provinces would merely find themselves free to reject. The hon. member will recall that in previous conferences the federal government had worked out positions jointly with one or several provinces thinking there was agreement, and then at the last minute the provinces would reject the whole package. We do not think that is a very profitable way to proceed.
By and large I have always said that the British North America Act is a pretty good one, that the basic framework of the constitution is still a pretty good one in my view. I have repeated the government's intention to be flexible. If the provinces see ways in which it can be improved, we see some ways, too. But we are not anxious to say that the constitution is not a good, basic framework. If the provinces want to make the case, we are prepared to discuss it with them and hear them out.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In light of his statement to the Congress about the sovereignty of parliament and the determination of Canadians to govern themselves with a parliamentary system, I ask if the Prime Minister does not think it would be useful to discuss in greater detail the up-to-date account of what changes are required, elicit the partnership of parliament and its members in dealing

with the threats to Canadian unity and thus expand on the message he gave the United States Congress?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CHANGES TO WHICH PRIME MINISTER REFERRED IN ADDRESS TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS-POSSIBILITY OF DEBATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, I would welcome debate on the subject, if the House would see fit to set aside time for that. I know the hon. member realizes, as we all do, that the matters to be dealt with are not purely or strictly constitutional. That is only one part of the whole series of accommodations which we must make within Canada in order to bind together even more tightly the Canadian people. The Leader of the Opposition was quoting some economic measures. There are social matters and other areas like immigration and communications which, without going into the constitution, might be the subject of administrative arrangement which would increase the bonds of national unity. So, I think it is rather difficult to reply to the hon. member only in terms of the constitution.

MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-POSSIBILITY OF PROCEEDING WITH CONSTRUCTION BEFORE ENERGY BOARD OR MR JUSTICE BERGER REPORT POSSIBILITY OF DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister regarding a press report in yesterday's paper from Washington. It reads:
Canadian officials indicated here Tuesday that Prime Minister Trudeau is ready to do all he can to speed a decision on the construction of a multi-million dollar Mackenzie Valley pipeline to carry Alaskan gas to Americans... the official said Trudeau explained to Carter that he would "like to be in a position not to embarrass him" over the pipeline.
In view of the fact that during this morning's CBC news, Mr. Lougheed, the Vice-President of Imperial Oil has taken these remarks to be what he calls "a favourable sign", I want to ask the Prime Minister if this assurance that the President is not going to be embarrassed represents a tacit understanding that Canada will proceed with the Mackenzie Valley pipeline despite the fact that neither the National Energy Board nor Mr. Justice Berger's report has yet been received?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-POSSIBILITY OF PROCEEDING WITH CONSTRUCTION BEFORE ENERGY BOARD OR MR JUSTICE BERGER REPORT POSSIBILITY OF DEBATE
speechtext:
I can say that anyone who would play the stockmarket on the basis of that remark would probably be very seriously financially embarrassed. What went on between President Carter and myself in the presence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was exactly as I have stated earlier in reply to a question from a

member of the Conservative Party. There were no guarantees of any particular pipeline. Indeed, there were no guarantees of any pipeline at all. There was an undertaking to study this whole question with a view to co-operating as much as we can with the United States, within the obligations we have to meet Canadian objectives, too. I spelt them out in some detail. Insofar as the words "embarrassing the President" are concerned, they were never used, Mr. Speaker, and no intention was there to use them. I do not believe I would be concerned about embarrassing him. He is a very eminent president and he can conduct his own affairs without my messing.

subtopic: MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-POSSIBILITY OF PROCEEDING WITH CONSTRUCTION BEFORE ENERGY BOARD OR MR JUSTICE BERGER REPORT POSSIBILITY OF DEBATE
speechtext: In view of the statement by what is alleged to be a Canadian official, that the Prime Minister assured the United States President that he would do everything he could to speed a decision, I want to ask the Prime Minister whether "speeding a decision" involves bypassing parliament. We are waiting for these. I do not know what decision will be taken, but if it is one which necessitates the government's coming before parliament, of course we will come before parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: PROPOSED REIMBURSEMENT OF PERSONS AGED 65 WHO LOST THEIR RIGHT TO BENEFITS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, first and foremost 1 think we should remember that some 600 individuals did in fact refuse to take their Quebec pension or Canada pension, did see fit to appeal and in fact won their appeal. speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: TELEVISION INDUSTRY TARIFF REMISSIONS
speechtext:
1. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce does not administer tariffs and thus has no power to remit duties. However, under the Financial Administration Act, the Governor in Council has the power to authorize Revenue Canada, Customs and Excise, to remit duties paid or payable in respect of goods imported into Canada. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has set into motion a programme, which under certain conditions, will permit the remission of duties on imported television receivers paid or payable by manufacturers of television sets in Canada. The purpose of this programme is to prevent an imminent failure of this industry sector which has neither the technology base nor scale to remain competitive in the Canadian market even with the current tariff of 15 per cent. Under the programme, television manufacturers who maintain at least a previous level of production with at least 50 per cent Canadian value added in their production will be allowed duty remission on sets which they import. The amount of duty remitted will be determined by the ratio of the value of their production to sales. This programme will allow Canadian manufacturers to specialize in those types of production that lead to improved efficiency. At the same time, the market share they obtain is not expected to change although they would no longer make a full range of T.V. products in Canada.
2.	(a) The department held negotiations with all Canadian television set manufacturers and with many of their parent companies with a view to increasing television production in Canada. No means was found to increase production in Canada that resulted in no higher costs to Canadian consumers, tax-payers or companies, (b) The new programme will include a Canadian value added requirement favouring the sourcing of components from Canadian component suppliers. Department officials have met with component manufacturers and are continuing to seek ways and means, in addition to the programme, to overcome the problems of a small domestic market.
3.	The department has taken no special measures in regard to layoffs at Renfrew Electric nor has the company or its employees approached the Department directly, asking for special measures. Officials of the department have expressed willingness to discuss Renfrew's situation with the company management with a view to assisting the firm to improve its position in the market place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as so many members have shown in this debate, the question posed by Bill C-37 is not only fiscal payments to the provinces for the next five years, already decided at the first ministers meeting' last December, but whether this bill is a sufficient response to the crisis of federalism. I said in the first part of

Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements my speech Tuesday night that Bill C-37 does not answer the real question in the relationship between Ottawa and the provinces. That is why so many members, in speaking during this debate, have responded to that deep yearning across the land for some leadership in parliament about the ways Canada can be held together. The Canadian people, fearful of the consequences of separation, need encouragement that members of parliament are at least sensitive to the dilemma. It is not the esoteric algebraic formulae in this bill that we should be debating. Rather, it is the future of confederation.
It is not good enough for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to go to Washington and assure the Americans that Canada will remain united. He has a duty to come into the House of Commons and tell Canadians precisely what he is going to do to keep Canada together. 1 think the questions that were raised in the House today on the Prime Minister's speech in Washington reflect the very deep concern of the members of the House that some serious statements be made right here in this forum about the government's plans for the accommodations that will be necessary to hold all the regions intact and to ensure the integrity of Canada. It is all very well to dazzle Washington, but it will take more than a high-flown speech to the U.S. Congress to settle the problems of regional alienation in this country.
There is no doubt that the Prime Minister opened the election campaign with his speech in Washington. That election is coming soon. The east block wizards are preparing their electronic electioneering to fool the Canadian people again; to make the people forget what miserable leadership they have had for the past nine years; to make them forget that this recycled architect of unity is the very man who has split the country apart; to make them forget that the deep problems of regional alienation are caused by this government's rigid centralism. But the Canadian people are not going to forget or forgive the damage done to our unity by this government.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) struck the central note in this debate. She
said:
It would be strange, indeed, if the parliament of Canada which so uniquely reflects the reality of federalism were to allow itself to be excluded from participating in the revitalization of that federalism. In the case of the bill before us today, parliament was relegated to the sidelines while these fiscal arrangements were being negotiated. Every time this happens, parliament is diminished-and at this critical time in Canada's history we need strengthened, not diminished, national institutions.
Advocating greater decentralization of the legislative and administrative systems through a national planning council that would develop a new national policy, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) said:
A truly national policy born of a consensus among all governments would, I believe, have a better chance of being accepted by the whole population because it would be more able to meet the objectives and priorities of each part of Canada.
That is a positive input into this debate that tells Canadians the direction in which the Progressive Conservative party is headed. The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) also enriched the debate from the perspective of the maritimes. He said:
The problem with which we must grapple, along with the complexities of this bill, is whether or not the arrangements which have been put before us and which were generally agreed to by the provinces in December hold out the danger of fundamentally increasing the sorts of disparities which exist now. When we look at the situation in the five eastern provinces specifically, and the swelling of the unemployment rate which has taken place in the past several months, we cannot be sanguine about this kind of proposed agreement and about the services which will be provided under this arrangement.
We want to be sure that the formula and framework which is being presented here will not be so rigid as to prevent effective action for dealing with disparities of income, employment, or unforeseen developments which may affect either existing revenues or bring about, indeed, a shortfall of revenues, or excessive costs in certain programs of the poorer provinces.
From the west we heard from the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) who pointed out:
This whole process of executive federalism, of dealing with the constitutional system of the country at only the highest and, in most cases, the most remote levels of government, belittles the House of Commons, renders the opposition meaningless, and contributes to a sense of high-level confrontations between political stars which heighten rather than reduce the centrifugal forces inherent in federal systems of government.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), another westerner, revealed his deep sense of Canadianism when he said:
We may be on the threshold of a new era of Canadian confederation, an era marked by greater awareness of provincial and regional needs and sensitivities, greater respect for the diversity of culture and heritage which characterizes the various parts of this country and, in the not too distant future, by a better
February 24, 1977

balance as between the centre and periphery of the country. This is the concept for which we must strive, in both official languages, and all regions.
Mr. Speaker, these are the speeches of leadership. Let no one say the opposition in this parliament only criticizes. We are leading the way into a renewed Canada. We do not need show business tactics. What we are doing is studying the options and creating new policies.
Mr. Speaker, around the world people are asking, "Can democracy cope with the complex problems of a modern, interdependent global community? There is a crisis of political faith in the ability of democratic governments to respond. All the polls indicate a serious dropping off of public belief in the efficacy and trustworthiness of government. Canada is by no means exempt from this voter disenchantment. Distrust of a large, powerful and faceless bureaucracy in Ottawa is intensifying. People are paying higher taxes than ever to support an ever-growing government-and yet the problems of transportation, housing and safety in society are getting worse. Decentralization is not a magic answer to all this, but without decentralization the problems of the municipalities, the level of government closest to the people, will become chaotic.
The rate of urbanization is nothing short of phenomenal. Before the end of this century 94 per cent of Canadians will be urbanized and three-quarters will live in 12 major cities. Urbanization is caused by an interlocking set of developments spawned by exploding technology. Government efforts must be directed toward managing the process of urbanization. The special problems of urbanization-public assistance, transportation, environmental management, leisure, recreation and housing-interact on one another and demand more money which municipalities have no way of raising, thus exacerbating their dependence on provincial and federal government grants.
The quality of life in urban centres is diminishing, despite local efforts; the institutional framework of government was established long before the social impact of urbanization was ever dreamed of. As the role and level of government in Canada has expanded, each level-federal, provincial and municipal-has become involved in areas in which the other levels previously had a special or exclusive interest. Complexity and fragmentation of government has followed. This has resulted in a proliferation of duplicative, autonomy-seeking special agencies in each level of government, and hence has highlighted the problem of a decision-making mechanism which can no longer respond to the needs of a society in an era of accelerating social change.
Thus, a new philosophy at the top is needed to meet the super problems of big government and urbanization. Only a new philosophy can counter the mounting evidence that government is big, rather than strong; flabby, rather than powerful; that is costs a great deal and does not achieve very much. More tinkering with government will not be enough. That is why the present federal government's policies on decentralization are inadequate. They are focused on spreading out certain government departments such as DREE, Revenue, and Supply and Services, and diversifying the sources of federal purchasing. This approach is too narrow a concept of decentralization.
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
A comprehensive plan based on a philosophy of streamlining is urgently needed-not more piecemeal solutions to mounting problems.
Decentralization is a theme running through the report on the constitution of Canada produced by the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in June, 1972. The committee made clear that we need a new constitution to make possible a more functional federalism. It stated:
A new Canadian constitution should be based on functional considerations, which would lead to greater decentralization of government powers in areas touching cultural and social policy and to greater centralization of powers which have important economic effects at the national level. Functional considerations also require greater decentralization in many areas of government administration.
The principal way in which constitutional decentralization can be brought about is contained in recommendation No. 50 which sets the division of powers in a more modern context as follows:
Concurrent powers which predominantly affect the national interest should grant paramountcy to federal parliament and those which predominantly affect provincial or local interests should grant paramountcy to the provincial legislature.
Therefore, a complete policy on decentralization begins with full support of the constitutional committee's recommendations on decentralization and a commitment to implement them. A more functional allocation of governmental powers will benefit all regions. The committee proposes an expansion of provincial powers in such areas as income support, criminal law, marriage and divorce, educational TV, taxing powers and international arrangements. The committee supports limitation of federal powers with respect to appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court and with respect to federal spending in fields of provincial jurisdiction. Correspondingly, greater centralization is necessary in the regulation of the economy. Hence, there should be a transfer of some existing provincial powers to the federal parliament; for example, an increase in federal jurisdiction over air and water pollution, international and interprovincial trade and commerce, incomes, securities regulation, financial institutions, unfair competition and foreign ownership.
The constitutional committee made a major recommendation concerning decentralization in the field of social security: the federal government should determine over-all spending in such programs as old age pensions, supplements and family allowances, and the provinces should determine how this total should be distributed within limits to preserve national standards and maintain the principle of redistributing income.
There is today a great deal of confusion over jurisdiction, and increasing political rivalry in promoting bigger social benefits. Integrated economic-social planning between the federal and provincial governments is imperative to prevent the escalation of universal benefits into a welfare state. Strategies for growth, housing and transportation are but three of the items in which the people will best be served by the three levels of government working closely together.

February 24, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
In considering ways to decentralization it should be reaffirmed that the federal parliament must retain the primary responsibility for general economic policy in the country. Thus, decentralization does not rule out centralization in primary areas. The federal parliament must have sufficient economic powers to regulate and influence the economy. However, in fulfilling this constitutional responsibility of centralization the federal government should explore more ways of decentralizing its operation so that federal policies can be regionally adapted. Decentralizing the decision-making process is of far more value than redistributing a handful of civil servants. The joint committee on the constitution of Canada recognized this and stated:
Most Crown corporations could have their headquarters outside Ottawa, as many already have. Federal departments like agriculture, energy, mines and resources, environment, national defence and transport could have their principal offices elsewhere, and many other departments could give their regional offices more authority. Even when Ottawa must remain the effective centre of administration, a greater effort can be made to encourage regional input.
Surely this was the thrust of the message of Newfoundland which we heard the other night from the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). To go to another part of the country, the western premiers, at the western economic opportunities conference, called for the establishment of industrial "centres of excellence" throughout the various regions of Canada. These centres would be based on natural and human resources, supported by research and marketing assistance to develop a vital economic unit capable of serving national and international markets.
Such a program concept suggests clear initiative on the part of the federal government in the establishment and support of new centres of industrial activity in Canada. It would involve decentralization of the technical expertise of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to plan and support the development of such centres, and the major funding of research activities and new industrial enterprise in co-operation with other departments of the federal government.
We can see, now, the necessity of the federal government permitting the provincial governments and various local organizations to participate in the planning of broad economic development policies, in establishing regional industrial priorities, and in the development and implementation of programs. There should be, in short, decentralization of decision-making power on assistance programs, and strengthening of regional offices. True decentralization calls for massive changes in the financial system of Canada so that municipalities can provide the public transportation, housing, water and social services demanded by urbanization. Grants by senior governments that want the political credit for handing out money are not the answer; today there are so many millions of dollars of transfer payments being issued from one government office to another that it is impossible to keep track of it all, let alone provide accountability to the people.
In summary, I do not see decentralization as a cure-all for Canada's problems and I am certainly not suggesting it as such, but it is an approach which will enable us to find the detailed answers Canada wants this place to find at this very
[Mr. Roche.)
critical moment in our history. It is time for us to assert our will to succeed as a people, for a nation is primarily constituted by its people's collective will to live together. In every region of Canada people have common aspirations for a truly human life. It ought to be the function of government and parliament to help all Canadians deepen faith in their own country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been an interesting debate, although sometimes one feels there is a certain sense of unreality because we cannot face up to the fundamental issues behind the bill just by the mere statistics and details of the legislation. While we defer consideration of the precise terms of the bill to a later stage, I was thinking as I glanced over this fundamental document that it might be something of an inadequate response to the challenge to confederation to look at something like	as one
of the formulae whereby we can work out the arrangements between the provinces and the dominion. That complicated formula cannot, of course, be the full and final answer, nor can we consider the clauses of the bill as sufficient discussion about the problem before us.
I have been impressed by those hon. members who have applied themselves to what I believe is the spirit of the law, as Montesquieu might say, and to the fundamental principles lying behind and beyond the law. I was notably impressed by the speeches of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the (Mr. Wagner). I was glad the Globe and Mail this morning showed the wisdom of reproducing his very helpful, very cognate and useful remarks. I cannot use her language now, but I thought the hon. lady made a masterful review of the situation, setting out fundamental truths and basic principles. I thought the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe made a moving statement of his credo on federalism. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands-and this has been referred to by an honourable, distinguished and learned gentleman, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche)-was profoundly correct when she pointed out the importance of this forum for discussion of great national issues.
As the House of Commons through the years has become something like a glorified sausage-mill of legislation we have tended to lose an understanding of its principal role. The House of Commons does not run the country; that is the job of the government. However, the House of Commons must, and should-and at its best, does-represent the country. So it is very important that in this body, which represents all the people and which is freely chosen by those people, we apply ourselves to fundamental questions. 1 was proud of the hon. lady for bringing forward that issue, and of the hon. gentleman for dealing with it.
This is the first time since the election in Quebec that there has been serious attention paid to that event. Without being an alarmist, I can say that Canada is in crisis. We are not asking just how we are going to be governed, or who is going to govern us-although that is important-but we are asking whether we will have a country tomorrow or at some not too
February 24, 1977

distant date. While the shock, uncertainty and anxiety which followed November 15 is the most serious crisis in our country's history, it is well for us not to regard it as the first one. We have had threats before-threats galore-and we should always remember that not all the threats to this nation have been uttered or written in French. We learn that in some parts of the western domain people are a little annoyed if they, too, are not counted in what is called alienation. We should remember that in fact our whole history has been a series of threats. As one of my professors used to say, there is this constant interplay between the centripetal and the centrifugal forces, one which would draw us together and the other which would pull us apart.
Before we began as a country, but after our forefathers began the discussion on the creation of a country, one province-New Brunswick-voted against it. It took clever manipulation to get them on the track so that by 1867 they were willing to come in. In Nova Scotia, the premier made sure that the people did not discuss the issue, did not vote on the issue, nor did the legislature vote on the issue. When confederation came in 1867, Nova Scotia sent a raft of members of parliament to the confederated capital, all but one of whom were dedicated to breaking up confederation. Long after that people in the maritimes could win elections on an anti-confederation plank. So it is not a new situation. But the country pulled together then to resist the storms and weather the anxieties and attacks.
At that time we had very wise men who saw that after you made a country, you had to do something to keep it together. Sir John A. Macdonald saw what I am afraid many people today are not seeing, and some of them bear the same party label as I do. He believed that the whole was greater than the parts and must be greater than the sum of the parts; that a strong central government with reserved power was absolutely necessary because that was the only critical mechanism which represented all the people of the total entity and which had at best the ability to inspire the ideals and patriotism of the people. He did more than that; he launched us on a program whereby we challenged our problems, our difficulties, our history and our geography. He did not mope and grope about internal strains. He set out a broad area of challenge. Perhaps today we are a little too inward-looking.
I have mentioned the past, Mr. Speaker, not because I am so old or old-looking, but I believe we ignore it at our peril. It has been said that a true Conservative derives lessons from the past and the reactionary is bound by them. We are not bound by the past, of course, but we serve ourselves ill if we forget it. I am not here to pretend that I am back in my university classroom. I am not here to administer a history lesson. 1 am here to express my concern about some of the developments in this country, and often I am a little more disturbed about the reactions to the events than to the events themselves.
I have read where it is said it is not inevitable that Quebec leave; that everything is going to be fine and all will be well in
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements the palsy-walsy world. I would say simply that it is not inevitable that they will not leave. There is no unwritten law that decrees we shall stay together. Much worse than that reaction is the reaction of those who say, "Let them go". That is a shocking, dangerous and, indeed, evil attitude for any Canadian to take. If there is no feeling of togetherness of people who have lived together and shared a country for over a century, then surely there is something terribly wrong.
Another suggestion we get is that Quebec cannot go. This is also dangerous. A state of Quebec would be no mean member of the community of nations. There are many perhaps a hundred-at the United Nations less capable and less viable economically than the province of Quebec. We should not build up illusions, nor should we foster narrow, bigoted attitudes that could be crippling and dangerous. 1 think it is important that we keep a sense of balance and a sense of moderation.
Another thing one hears is that if there is successful separation of Quebec, it will be followed by withdrawal of other units. This I find to be the lowest common denominator of national faith. Surely, if it should happen-and pray God it will not-that one of our prime members should leave, should not, and would not, all the other members draw more closely together instead of flying off into different areas? So I am not impressed by the suggestion that that would shatter our national dream still further in respect of others following the example. I cannot believe that patriotic Canadians, whether east, west, centre or farther, would believe in such an unworthy suggestion.
We cannot stand idly by and see separatism manipulated or stumbled into by demagogues or ill-advised zealots. It is our duty, to use an old-fashioned word, to keep this country together. I would not for a moment suggest that I am a better Canadian than anyone in this chamber or anyone in this country, but one of my great honours is to represent the cradle of confederation. I represent the place where it all began in 1864-Charlottetown. I do not want to see the dreams of those forefathers shattered in my lifetime. 1 do not want to see the great entity which they created destroyed in my lifetime or the lifetime of my children.
On the plaque of the confederation chamber in Charlottetown is a typical Canadian attitude, part of a verse from an American writer and part from an English writer, which reads:
Providence being their guide.
They builded better than they knew.
I have spent much of my life decrying the denigration of our founding fathers, the unwillingness to recognize them as among the greatest nation-builders in the world. With all the gravity at my command I would like to give my humble views on how we, as Canadian legislators dealing with the matter of federal-provincial relations, which is the essence of the federal system, can deal with something which is so important to us. First, we cannot do it by force. That would be unthinkable and probably impossible, if we were foolish enough to think of it. We do not have to look any further than to Lebanon or

February 24, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
Northern Ireland to see the criminal folly of fratricidal blood-letting.
We cannot do it by fear. We hear it said, "They will never make it alone. They cannot do it economically." That will not help. It is a delusion. I think we can no more solve this situation by balance-sheets than we can by battalions. We cannot do it by confrontation, either. I differ strongly with those who say the best thing is to have a national referendum and let the whole country vote. That would polarize one against the other. We do not need polarization; we need accommodation; we need agreement.
The final thing that concerns me is that we cannot save this country by so diminishing the central government that there is nothing left but a loose alliance of dominion states. To so weaken the central government as to make it meaningless would be a defeat by default. We need to recognize mutual problems.
When I first came to this chamber 20 years ago, the fourth edition of Beauchesne's had been printed. Mr. Beauchesne was not a Scotsman. Members of the House who spoke French only and became involved in procedural arguments-they are difficult enough even when you know the English language- could only use the English version of Beauchesne because it had not been translated into French. It was not translated until 1964 although it was written in 1922. Also, at that time we who were not wise enough or fortunate enough to understand French could not understand what our French-speaking colleagues said because there was no translation system. And all this took place nearly 100 years after the country began, a country which began by saying clearly, as the British North America Act said, that the two languages are equal in the parliament of Canada. If they are equal in the parliament of Canada, would it not be logical to make the whole apparatus on which parliament rests reflect that bilingual equality? There have been great anxieties over the Official Languages Act and its implementation. But part of our trouble today is that we have tried to put right in ten years that which has been neglected for 100 years. We who are Anglophones in this House must remember these things and take cognizance of them.
I agree with much that has been said previously about the need for less bitterness in dominion-provincial relations, about the need for greater accommodation on many matters. 1 agree with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said a couple of hours ago, that the British North America Act is a pretty fine document. I think it is capable of great flexibility. Nova Scotia, through Joseph Howe, had it changed in a matter of months. Certain subsidies were written in. As I say, great accommodation is possible. 1 think the old document is fine. But if it be necessary to change the constitution in order to keep the country, let us change the constitution. A certain Protestant French prince once said that Paris was worth a Mass.
I think the British North America Act is a fine document, repatriated or not. But surely the country is far greater than the BNA Act. If in the process of bringing about new beginnings and deeper understandings it needs to be changed, so be it. In these days of instant communication, easy transportation, electronic media and sophistication, surely it is easier for us to keep this magnificient, modern country together than it was for our forefathers to structure a union between dissociated, dislocated, remote communities in a primitive age, when there was little certainty as to how great our future would be in material terms. I say our job should be easier. I believe that if we fail in that, if we become wreckers of confederation instead of fathers of confederation, we shall be unworthy of them and unworthy of ourselves.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977   MEASURE FOR MAKING CERTAIN FISCAL PAYMENTS AND OF ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-37, an act to provide for the making of certain fiscal payments and of establishing programs covering financial contributions to the provinces. I particularly welcome the opportunity to speak immediately following my esteemed colleague for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie) for, like him, on June 10, of this year I shall have served this House for 20 years. In that time I know both of us have seen many changes in the country and in the House.
This bill is important and complex and comes before the House when there is much soul-searching in Canada. Scarcely a day passes without members of parliament, presumably of all parties, receiving letters from their constituents asking, "What has gone wrong in Canada? Where did we take the wrong turn in the road? How did we lose our way?" For example, our senior citizens are worried and concerned because the purchasing power of their savings has been eroded to the point where they may be unable to provide for their own physical needs in old age. Our young and middle-aged citizens are frustrated and perplexed by their inability to pay high interest and mortgage payments, by the inadequacy and high cost of housing and by the fear that no matter how hard they work they will never get out of debt. Our young people, to use the vernacular, can no longer "get with it," for the youth of our country represents the largest percentage of unemployed on our unemployment rolls.
We must ask ourselves, what does Bill C-37 do for them and what does it do to alleviate the present crisis in our nation, a crisis which is eating at our very vitals morning, noon and night? Unfortunately, it does little. This bill represents an agreement made between Canada's first ministers last December and attempts to bring about substantial changes in fiscal responsibilities and government programs applying to our two levels of government without seeking any formal amendment of our constitution.
As was said so ably by my leader and other colleagues, especially the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the premiers have been quoted as being in agreement with these proposals. But what else could they do? When you have a gun at your head and you need financial help, what else can you do? There was no way the premiers were going to throw their weight around and refuse the bone thrown to them. Since

February 24, 1977

1 realize that Nova Scotia, my own province, needs every cent it can get, I intend to vote for this bill. But the manner in which it was conceived leaves much to be desired. To be frank, it seems to me that more problems of national import are examined and finalized in Ottawa's old railway station than in the House of Commons by Canada's elected representatives.
Apparently this is the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) concept of co-operative federalism. Unfortunately, the concept has failed and a new approach to our problems must be found if we are to go forward in unity as a nation. Perhaps the Prime Minister's greatest failure in this, our hour of crisis, has been failure of communication. For far too long this elitist, selfseeking, overindulgent government has been practising a policy of confrontation rather than of consultation. We have had confrontations with labour, business, management-with just about every segment of society, in which 1 include our provincial governments. Today our provincial governments are confronted with a "take it or leave it" attitude in revenue sharing. Our provincial governments are being asked to reduce the cost of their administrations by our pyromaniac Prime Minister who, having ignited the inferno, now asks the premiers to dampen the fires of inflation. This "con" artist has developed a lifestyle at public expense which would put an Arabian oil sheik to shame-a swimming pool, massive staff, Cadillacs- you name it, he's got it! After emptying the public purse to the tune of some $5 billion this year alone, he has the gall to ask the premiers to practise restraint. Some members of parliament seem to be unaware of this government's waste and extravagance. However, a short review of the record will soon establish the facts. According to the tables the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury) presented to this House in 1974 when he was president of the treasury board, tables contained in the pamphlet entitled "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent", in 1967-68 when the present government was elected under the leadership of our present Prime Minister it took less than $10 billion to look after the needs of 20 million Canadians, or about $1 billion for every two million citizens. Now, ten years later, there are some 23 million Canadians. Using the same yardstick of $1 billion for two million citizens our budget should be in the order of $12.5 billion or, if I allow for inflation, about $13 billion. However, as we are all painfully aware, the budget is not $13 billion, $20 billion, $25 billion, $30 billion, $35 billion or even $40 billion-it is in excess of $45 billion.
Is it any wonder that Canadians of all ages are worried, or that the bonds which unite us have become frayed and torn? No nation, no matter how strong, can long survive this type of internal pressure. Just as families start feuding and fighting and breaking up when problems of money, or lack of money, become a central issue, I believe the same is true of the nation.
With the tabling of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1978, it is now obvious that it is not the intention of the government to treat the provinces fairly or justly or with due consideration for their economic needs. To realize the truth of that statement all one needs to do is compare the
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements amount earmarked for public works in the Atlantic region with the amount which is spent by the Department of Public Works in the national capital region of Ottawa-Hull. The Atlantic region is to receive some $14.5 million, while Ottawa-Hull is to enjoy the benefit of approximately six times as much-some $87.9 million. Incidentally, Quebec is to receive around $128 million.
The federal energy department and its agencies are to have its total spending trimmed by some $500 million. But how is this to be accomplished? Most of the so-called saving will be the result of a projected $612 million cut in oil subsidy payments to the five eastern provinces. The federal so-called savings will thereby be financed by the people of Atlantic Canada who will be paying more for energy. This is the end result of the government's freeze on expenditures. The only ones who may freeze next winter will be the people of Atlantic Canada suffering under the policies of this administration.
In addition, the citizens of Atlantic Canada will be paying more next year in health and welfare costs since this government plans to cut its contribution to our region by around 2 per cent. It is interesting to note, also, that our unemployed have not been forgotten. The cut in the budget of the Unemployment Insurance Commission is bound to wreak more hardship on an area already suffering from a hopelessly high rate of unemployment. So what will happen? If neither jobs nor benefits are available for our people, we cannot, in all conscience, let them starve. They will have to turn to the local welfare rolls, thus placing a further burden on our municipalities, an elected level of government which has the lowest level of tax sources available to it.
Granted, the government plans to set aside around $286 million for a project designed to create jobs and train those who are out of work. I submit the announcement is not impressive when viewed in the context of what has happened in the past in the field of job-creation and training. In my opinion, what is needed is an entirely new approach to economic growth. In the past, grants have been made to business by a government department following an assessment of the future of the firm concerned. This assessment was carried out by public servants. In effect, the government has decided that public servants can take better decisions in the business world than can the businessmen themselves. This, of course, is nonsense, for if public servants really possessed this kind of expertise they would hasten to establish their own businesses. All the system has done is build up a bureaucracy while adding to the burden placed upon successful business ventures which in the end must provide the tax dollars to the government.
I believe the government should provide encouragement for businessmen to start new enterprises without direct government interference. One way to do this would be to establish a standard grant formula under which any firm setting up or expanding an enterprise would be entitled to assistance amounting to a certain percentage of the costs up to a fixed maximum. The government's role would only be to determine that the criteria specified in legislation were met by the

February 24, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements participating firm. The grants would then be automatic. There would be no need for an army of bureaucrats trying to assess business factors. The evidence that a businessman, or a group of businessmen, showed willingness to risk capital in an endeavour would be taken and accepted as an indication of a favourable business assessment.
There is another method which might be used. The government could provide a tax incentive, something which would require even less bureaucracy. What 1 have in mind is a proposal that any person investing equity capital in a new or expanding business could write off a certain percentage of that amount against tax liability. The government would share the risk, as it does now, with a grant but under my plan the business decisions would be left to the private entrepreneur. Such an approach would be even more helpful to our young people with new ideas. They would be able to attract equity capital from other citizens, each of whom would make his own assessment of the viability of the project. Additional business judgment would thus be brought to bear on each new enterprise, adding to the probability that the business would be successful.
There are, undoubtedly, other equally valid proposals that could be made, but the key element in my suggestion is that the government would no longer be making business judgments and assessments. I submit that business assessments are not the function of government. This is, and must, remain the function of private enterprise if our system is to survive. 1 am not saying that the government should wash its hands of the entire matter and get out of the field of economic growth. What 1 am suggesting is a change in the government's role. The government can create the environment in which private enterprise, big and small businesses, can flourish. Experience over the years has shown that businessmen, if given half a chance, will start a new enterprise or expand an existing one if they can see a profit in so doing. I know, because I am speaking from experience.
The government can help by providing information on markets foreign and local. In fact, businessmen respond to opportunities for making a profit, and profit is only possible if goods or services can be sold. The federal government could provide some of this market by moving more of its government offices to areas of high unemployment such as the Atlantic region. In addition, the federal government, with its vast, persuasive powers, could help encourage the large labour-intensive administrative head offices of our insurance companies, trust companies, banks and labour organizations to locate in slow growth or high unemployment areas. This was not feasible in the past, but today we can communicate within seconds with men on the moon, or a spaceship on Mars-so modern communication systems make it possible to locate head offices anywhere in Canada.
In addition to these proposals, the federal government simply has to continue its equalization and transfer payment programs. These have been the main instruments for improving our business environment in the past. In my opinion, these

programs should not be reduced at least until more positive economic conditions in our area have been created.
Throughout my remarks I have endeavoured to relate our present national plight to our economic plight. I believe that if steps are taken along the lines I have proposed to strengthen our economic situation we will at the same time strengthen our national unity. From the letters I receive from my constituents, it is obvious that they and the vast majority of people in Canada are concerned about the current political health of our country. There is pessimism throughout the land that I find unrealistic and defeatist in its attitude.
It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada. I, for one, believe he was right. However, if we are to get on with the task of nation-building, we must rekindle our faith in our national destiny. Our very survival as a nation has been because of our diversity. Each of us has inherited, and has been enriched by, the contributions made throughout Canada by a number of cultural groups. Today, I believe that each of us as individual citizens must develop a new sense of personal dedication and participation in the future of our country. The preservation and the development of Canada must be beyond political parties, beyond factions and beyond selfish interests. In my view, it must be done through the wholehearted co-operation of Canadians of all political views, all languages and racial origin.
Without this commitment on the part of the individual Canadian for his country, and for the ideals for which it stands, without the direct participation of individual Canadians in the decisions that will seriously affect this nation's future, the decisions unfortunately will be made by competing provincial governments, self-seeking politicians and a few powerful special interest groups. This simply must not happen. The job of reaffirmation to Canadian ideals, the job of reconfederation-that is the task that faces us-will have to be done within Canada and by all Canadians. It is a job that cannot be done by the temporary managers of our society. It is a job that will be done, a job that must be done, by the owners of our society, namely, the citizens of Canada.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977   MEASURE FOR MAKING CERTAIN FISCAL PAYMENTS AND OF ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall confine my remarks on this complex bill to two or three phases which I believe are the most important, at least in principle; namely, what the government is doing in terms of financing in the health field. In a general way we support the thrust of the government's legislation in this regard. Since I came to this House I have been of the opinion that the federal government should by and large not be involved in the financing of health, welfare and post-secondary education, at least to any massive degree. Rather, this should be done by the provinces and returned to them at the earliest opportunity, with appropriate tax concessions.
I think this practice is a monster which has been built up largely at the instigation of the federal government. I remember that in 1969 the Weir government in Manitoba, the last Conservative government in the province, tried to negotiate
February 24, 1977

with the federal government some type of control over medicare which would not be onerous to its citizens, yet were rebuffed by the federal government. We now have a quite massive program which has to be curtailed. I also believe that these financing programs have been one of the main causes of the threatened break-up of confederation because of their economic effect.
Before the advent of shared-cost programs in the field of health, welfare and post-secondary education Canadians lived with a great deal of national identity. In view of the affluence of the times it would appear that these programs should have brought Canadians closer together, whereas in fact they have separated them. Having been given vast sums of money to spend on health, welfare and education-and since 20 years ago each community has been largely responsible for its own level of education, medical and hospital care-this has now become the responsibility of the distant federal government. Even 25 years ago 80 per cent of local education costs up to university level was raised from property taxes, and virtually all Canadians paid for their own doctor and hospital care either out of their own pockets or under a plan from which they could draw no more than they had paid in by way of premiums. The shared-cost programs under which the federal government paid 50 cents on the dollar encouraged great expansion of the health and welfare fields, as well as education. Indeed, if the amount spent on health and welfare by the federal government were taken out of the budget, the budget would be quite manageable.
It is often thought by Canadians that their economic problems are unique, whereas in fact they are largely problems experienced in the English-speaking world. They are problems largely invented by Canadian public opinion and policy in the frequent and fallacious Canadian attempt to arrive at a national identity by perpetuating mistakes made by the two larger nations that we most envy and resemble, at least in our social structure, namely, Great Britain and the United States.
The central problem is the runaway welfare state whose Canadian identity is closer to that of Britain than the United States. One of the main problems was the adoption by the Canadian government of the Marsh report, a report written by Leonard C. Marsh in 1943 on social security in Canada. It was patterned after the Beveridge plan and it rested on the assumption that "cradle to the grave" social security would not undermine but would, instead, reinforce the traditional personal and social values of self-reliance and devotion to hard work. It was not realized that as new generations replaced the old and as people became used to the welfare state they would regard social security as their due; that work was only a means of qualifying for such, or a source of discretionary income and that in fact this discretionary income would increasingly not be worth working too hard for since it would be heavily taxed for the benefit of others.
Along with the social benefits of health and welfare, the commitment of the government to maintain high employment assumed that people would remain grateful for the employment and would not take advantage of the guarantee to seek
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements higher wages, either by exploitation of monopoly power by powerful unions or by shifting part of the burden of taxes to other shoulders.
Inherent in this legislation is a discussion on where education is tending to go. The emphasis on the democratic right to free higher education has meant keeping a large part of the population in school during the period of young adulthood, where previously it would have had to start a career with reasonable lifetime prospects. This would not be so bad if school is serious hard work which drives a student to acquire useful productive skills. But in the three English-speaking nations I referred to, the self-fulfilment ideas of the teacher and the minimum effort objectives of the students combine to produce an incipient labour force that is well prepared to consume income and well-schooled in administering a job but has frequently missed the experience of exerting one's abilities to the limit in mastering the work involved. There is an important difference in the conception of the old idea of working and the modern idea of having a job.
The extension of the generous state-financed pensions to the retired is most widely acclaimed on the basis that it was the least objectionable aspect of the welfare state because it recognized that many old people could not work and could not fend for themselves. The advent of the old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and the Canada pension, plus the scourge of the elderly-the great fear that a man would be unable to care for himself, to pay for his drugs, for hospital care and for his doctor-has removed from the citizen the requirement of savings, retirement funds and pensions which have contributed substantially to the inflationary pressures that are now upon us.
I have often said that it is not necessary to have nearly the personal savings now as it was a few years ago, and the consuming portion of old age is not nearly as important as it was. For these people the problems of health are paramount. Earlier retirement and increasing attention to young adults programs are increasingly dividing the population into two groups of consumers, one young, one old, supported by an in-between adult group of producers carrying a heavy burden of taxation.
The most important features of the enormous government increase in expenditure are in the field of health, welfare and education. With the advent of the government-sponsored plans, costs have escalated enormously. Certainly, the government of the sixties that instituted these plans must bear a great deal of criticism for the state of our economy. Much of the thinking on entering these state-run plans was misdirected, but entirely understandable. I cannot help thinking of a clause or manifesto of the British Labour party which suggested that all sickness was the result of inadequate medical care. The paper debated by the Labour party permitted the idea that through better medical care the need for hospitals would gradually dry up and they could be closed. Indeed, modern medicine that reduces death and illness in earlier life only prolongs the

February 24, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements lifespan so that the degenerative diseases of heart, cancer and plain old age bring the medical problems of the individual to much greater importance, and the financial obligations of the state are immensely increased.
The BN A Act, as I understand it, gave to the provinces health, welfare and education, and they should return there as quickly as possible. In my opinion, the so-called equality of medical and hospital care is highly overrated. An analysis of hospital care shows that it is becoming rigid. Hospitals are being run for the staff and the administration, with the patients being of secondary importance. They are only necessary to keep jobs for the staff. If one studies the hospital policy, it is obvious that the number of people actually involved in the care of patients is not a great deal more than what it was when patients paid for their own care. The great expansion has been in the ancillary and the administrative spheres. Many jobs in the periphery of hospitals are hard to justify. Mostly the problem with these programs is that there are no guidelines, no limits that may be reasonably imposed on medical, hospital and educational institutions. There are always new and endless programs that will benefit some in the community and certainly some that one has to consider as very worthwhile. It is very difficult to give up a program once instituted. It is always easier to try to start another program.
With the provinces having to finance and run their own programs, we can expect to have more efficiency and more innovation. There should not be the same drive to innovate new programs merely because some other province had them and that province needed them in order to save face. Perhaps the provinces, in turn, will involve once more local governments and even voluntary groups in the administration and financing of hospitals and medical care. The smaller the political unit, the much better the spending power used. It seems to me that municipal government gets more "bang for their buck" than the provincial government, and the provincial government seems to spend better than the federal government, at least in productivity for the amount of money spent. I believe that the federal government must negotiate in good faith. It must return these programs to the care of the provinces. I come from a province that receives some money. I understand that on balance the province of Manitoba neither gains nor loses much in the exchange.
The question of unity has been touched on in this debate by many people, most pointedly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). The election of Mr. Levesque has once more brought the country to considering the constitution and the make-up of confederation. Now that Quebec has forced the issue, the country cannot go back again. Suffice it to say the new mood in Quebec and in the other provinces has shifted dramatically against the federalism of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Now, in 1977, if the issues are debated more calmly I think they are more dangerous. For the past number of years the government's very narrow and bilingual policies, which was the approach to Quebec nationalism, have increasingly come to be disputed and distrusted by English Canada, and growing skepticism of the value of Ottawa's bilingual

policies and the independence of Quebec has become a subject of consideration. If the country is to avoid political disaster, it needs the good will of English-speaking Canada.
It is doubtful if this government has the capacity to meet this crisis. If they had a policy and if it was aimed at anything, it was at preventing the Parti Quebecois from coming to power. However, the Parti Quebecois is now in power and Mr. Bourassa is studying arrangements for the Common Market in Brussels. Obviously, Ottawa's Quebec policy has failed. How can it be expected, unless that policy is changed, to overcome the PQ in power, and can this government, with its tight commitment to the central role, shift its faith and perspectives sufficiently to meet the changed circumstances? If there is to be a national policy capable of coming to terms with Quebec nationalism, it must be one which represents and asserts the will of English-speaking Canada to live for itself also as an independent community. If Quebec is to be granted the choice over its destiny, there must be a collective future awaiting the provinces and territories that remain. Will these diverse provinces be able to live together? The government has been in office a long time and it has a massive federal bureaucracy to back it up. If a federal government, made up of half of its members from the province of Quebec and one-third of its cabinet ministers from that province is unable to prevent the election of a Parti Quebecois government, then one has to conclude that the electorate, in electing Mr. Levesque, represents strong feelings on the part of the Quebecois.
There are those in the federal cabinet, including the Minister of Finance, who have suggested that provincial premiers who join Quebec in a united front during federal-provincial conferences make themselves accomplices to the PQ cause. The Prime Minister has said that the federal system is untouchable-"to abandon it now would be a sin against the spirit, to sin against humanity". These are hardly words by which politicians would be ready to enter an open and reasonable discussion on constitutional changes.
The province of Quebec has set its sights on independence, while Canada seems to be failing to search for the appropriate language, constitutional devices and the mechanism of change that will guide us. We have to respond to the challenge of Quebec with prudence and thought. All seem agreed that the new shape of things must envisage more independence for the province of Quebec. But what forms remain for the rest of the Canadian confederation?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977   MEASURE FOR MAKING CERTAIN FISCAL PAYMENTS AND OF ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in the debate on Bill C-37. However, having listened to hon. members put forth their views and then using the bill as a springboard to discuss the whole question of Canadian confederation, and what has taken place in the last two days, I am moved to at least say a few words on this question. I can promise Your Honour that it will not last six hours.
We in this party oppose Bill C-37. We have argued that, in effect, once it is implemented, the poorer provinces in this
February 24, 1977

country will suffer as a result of it and will feel the effects even more severely than the wealthy provinces which can sustain that sort of impact. But more than that, since this bill comes at a very important time in the development of the history of Canada, one thing that concerns me greatly is the colonialist mentality which we as Canadians still seem to have.
I recognize the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was following the long tradition of potential actors and performers who have to go to the United States to become successful and who then bring back their success to Canada. While 1 recognize the quality of his speech, I would have appreciated it far more had it been made in Canada to Canadians, because in effect the problems facing us as Canadians today must be solved by Canadians. We are the ones who will have to solve the problems, instead of running to Big Brother in the hope that Big Brother will help us in this game to solidify Canadian unity. It seems to me to be betraying a colonialist mentality which we have not yet outgrown. 1 refer in particular to the comment made by the Primer Minister at the press conference when he said:
The greatest threat to the United States is the disintegration or the break-up of Canada.
It struck me immediately, as I read it, as being a tacit invitation to Big Brother. Here is the Prime Minister, the leader of a country, saying in effect to our neighbour that their security depends on Canada being united. So if, for example, Mr. Levesque and the Parti Quebecois are seen as endangering that unity, it is not beyond the realm of possibility that all sorts of agents, agents provocateurs, CIA and other characters will want to invade this country in an effort to destabilize the situation in Quebec. Indeed, it is an open invitation to American investors to stay out of the province of Quebec, thus creating a situation of hardship in Quebec so as to bring the people of that province to realization of the error of their ways and so as to convince them not to support separation in any referendum.
I say that the people of Quebec made their choice, and they had the democratic right to do so. I think it really puts me down as a Canadian when the leader of my country goes to the capital of a foreign country and makes a press statement in which he says, in effect, "Boys, the greatest threat to the United States of America would be the break-up of Canada".

The only way that can come about is for Canada to be free. From my ideological perspective, we should have a free socialist Canada because, in my view, that
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements is the only way in which Canada can guarantee the cultural rights of all groups within Canada and of all provinces.
I hear giggling on my right, but the fact remains that foreign ownership in Canada is still a great threat. What is the good of coming through the other struggle as a united Canada when, in effect, we have no control over our consumer patterns and no control over our own culture, when the culture we have is by and large a foreign culture and when our standard of living is based on what is happening in the United States so that when they have a tough time we have an even tougher time. We must be able to say to Canadians that we want a free and independent Canada, but that to achieve it we will have to make some sacrifices. Yes, we will even have to be prepared to accept a lower standard of living as we try to achieve some economic independence and, we hope, the cultural independence which will follow.
What we have done is, in effect, to give up that whole fight. There was a great froufra about foreign ownership in this country, so we brought in the Foreign Investment Review Act.
I have received reports which state that six out of seven applications for take-overs are approved. As parliamentarians, we never see the basis for an approval or a rejection of a take-over. We see the spectacle of provincial premiers running to the boardrooms in foreign countries begging them to invest in their provinces.
Coming, as I do, from a colony and having seen the republics in the south and how they develop, I know that the investors will come in, but they will come in for a price, which is the loss of sovereignty. You lose the right to direct the way your country will eventually develop. To me, that is very important. That is an argument which we have to make in Canada, and the Prime Minister and those of us who are committed to an independent, united Canada must attempt to convince Canadians that there is a benefit in being in Canada which is united and independent, in spite of what it might cost us in terms of our standard of living.
I wanted to put those few remarks on the record because I think they are very important. They have been running through my mind since the Prime Minister's speech in the U.S. Congress and his press conference in Washington, and because everybody is basking in some sort of aura, saying to themselves, "The American senators love us. Aren't we just great? We have really come of age." Quite frankly, what the American senators think and do is their business and they have the right to run their own affairs, but I think we should balance out the picture because we are getting carried away and are basking in the euphoria of the success of the great speech made in Congress.
