speechtext:
All the taxpayers. That is really the point. I presume the hon. gentleman would like to separate the taxpayers of the various provinces. They make contributions to Ottawa and the government goes back to an arrangement. Through discussions, those arrangements are agreed to by the parties. This time they were not.
There has been a desire on the part of the federal government to limit such things as hospital costs, medical costs and post-secondary education costs. The federal government pretty well took a unilateral position. It is true that the provinces were there and agreed, but most of them did so because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said that the deadline was March 31. He told the provinces that the federal government had to have this agreement by then or they would not get any, and that from then on they would get only what the federal government wanted to give them.
February 24, 1977

1 talked to a young French Canadian chap the other day and asked him if he really felt he was a Canadian or if he felt his nationality was that of a Quebecker. He said that he was a Quebecker. However, he said that it was funny, but his mother does not feel that way. I asked him why, and he said it was for the simple reason that his mother gets her old age pension cheque from Ottawa, that she looks to Ottawa as being the central government and that she has a relationship with it. I asked the young fellow whether that meant his mother has a Canadian attitude. He said, "No, just Ottawa, because the money comes from there." However, that money is Canadian money, put in by all the provinces and redistributed. That is really what federalism has been all about: the strong areas help the weak areas.
I come from the richest province of Canada, the province of Ontario, and yet the area I come from has some of the most abject poverty in the country. The poverty in northern Ontario is worse than the poverty in many of the smaller provinces which we consider to be have-not provinces. We have that poverty because there is not really any redistribution. In areas like that we count on redistribution by the central government operating on behalf of all the people. However, we should tell everybody that. We should tell them so they know Canada has some meaning to them and so they can relate. They would then know when they drive over the Trans-Canada Highway that half its cost is paid for by people in other parts of Canada. We should tell them that when they go to the hospital, half the expenses are paid by the federal government. The federal government also pays half the cost of all medical plans.
We should not have a situation where there is a Quebec Pension Plan and a Canada Pension Plan. We should have one pension plan, and that plan should be for the benefit of all Canadians regardless of where they live. As long as there has been a Liberal government or a Union Nationale government in the province of Quebec there has always been a willingness on the part of the federal government to treat Quebec differently. My party has been no different. We have considered the idea of a special status; we have considered the two-nation theory; we have tried them all. What we should really have been trying to do was develop Canadianism. That idea has never really been adopted because of the way money is given to the province of Quebec.
Many times in this House the former leader of the Social Credit party of Canada, the late Real Caouette, spoke about the educational system. He used to say that our educational system should be directed toward developing a Canadianism which would enable all Canadians to feel at home in all parts of the country. He agreed with the suggestion which was made by other people-a suggestion I agreed with for a long time- that the only way to promote unity in a bilingual sense would be to put money into the elementary school level in Quebec and every other province.
That should not be done by force, however, because if it is we are going to lose one province or another. It should be done in such a way that everyone at the elementary level in Canada could have the advantage of learning two languages. That is
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements the only difference there is between Canada and the United States. The United States adopted the melting-pot system whereby everybody became American and spoke English. We have had two languages in Canada for 300 years. We have allowed the use of those languages, where possible, in all government departments. But, Mr. Speaker, we went further than that; we allowed a lot of other languages. In Ottawa schools probably four or five different languages are taught. I know many young people who have gone to public school after the regular hours to learn the language of their parents, and there is nothing wrong with that. It has helped us develop our Canadian identity. There is nothing wrong with the bilingualism program itself-just the slavish position taken by the government on providing bilingualism by force to civil servants when it should be voluntary and available to everyone.
I watched a program in Ottawa recently about a fight over bilingualism in an Ottawa school. The fight was not about bilingualism in the particular classroom but about whether there would be an influx of other children to that school and then the bilingual children would have to be removed and sent to a school a mile and a half away. It should be easy to solve that problem by making bilingualism available in all schools, surely. The price may be that the federal government should put up the money for bilingual education.
I would also want to make bilingual education available in every school in Quebec. I am not in favour of asking everyone else to be bilingual and leaving Quebec unilingual, and I do not think that is the wish of the majority of the people in the province. It has certainly never been the practice in Ontario. The people I represent are 30 per cent French-speaking and about only 100 of them are not fluently bilingual.
The federal government should co-operate with the provinces and provide the money for bilingual training. It seems to me that, as one hon. member said, the government has always treated this matter in the old "union station" manner rather than in parliament. It is like one horse and one rabbit; when the government starts negotiating with the provinces, what weapon have the provinces got? The federal government has the money, and the provinces ask for their share but they have to take whatever is given to them. Over the years they have been able to get a few concessions, but all of a sudden the government says, "We do not have that kind of money now to meet all the 50-50 plans for health, medicare, post-secondary education and some other projects, so we are going to put on a ceiling and change the rules." How do provincial premiers or ministers of finance go to the old Union Station and say, "There is no way you are going to do that to us?" In the last round of negotiations they were told to take it or leave it, and if they did not take it by the end of March a decision would be made for them.
I would not object to the federal government making that decision unilaterally provided they said so and were willing to designate what they were paying the money for. We have to develop an attachment to the Canadian idea, to the Canadian

Mr. Speaker in joining in this debate I should like to touch on three basic themes.
I should like to touch, first of all, on the fact that I believe- and many of my colleagues believe-that it is important in Canada today that there be a restructuring of the levels of government and their responsibility. Second, I should like to touch on the unfortunate urban transit reneging that has taken place at the federal government level. The commitment given to the Canadian public in 1974 to spend $290 million to assist municipalities and provinces with their urban transit needs has been reneged. I should like to give some further details of the implications that has for certain provinces, in particular my own province of Ontario. Third, in this general discussion I should like to look at what has happened with respect to federal government expenditures, what has been the restraint shown at the federal level, and to what degree has the federal government simply loaded on to other jurisdictions a still heavier load as far as financing needs are concerned in future than has been the experience for those municipalities and provinces up to the present time?
Dealing first with the topic of restructuring, 1 believe that most members of the House would agree that the day is coming when the Canadian public, Canadian taxpayers-who,
[Mr. Peters.J
after all, foot the bill whether it is municipal tax, provincial or federal tax-will insist that there be less duplication, less overlapping of governmental services than exists today. I think the federal government could take the lead in inviting the various levels of government to some type of conference where this overlapping could be reviewed.
Let me cite some examples where, surely, it would be fruitful to have discussions between provincial and federal governments to see, for example, if the overlapping cannot be restructured by either leaving a program or department at the federal level or leaving it at the provincial level-but, in any event, not allowing the programs to be duplicated at so many levels of government as is the case at the present time. In talking to municipal and provincial officials I have found that the situation is at the point where it is literally counterproductive. For example, officials of the Department of the Environment in Ottawa draw up plans and make pfoposals for solving environmental problems, but they find that there is a similar bureaucratic structure at the provincial level. The two sets of bureaucrats seem to spend most of their time debating with each other whose plan is correct. In the meantime, nothing is done to solve the environmental problem. We find that the hiring at the federal level of relatively senior bureaucrats at relatively high salaries triggers the hiring at both provincial and municipal levels of high price bureaucrats who do jobs similar to those of their federal counterparts, the idea being that the two levels of bureaucracy can deal with one another on an equal footing. But the sad part is that the taxpayers of the country, whom we have the honour to represent, must pay for this relatively non-productive activity.

I say we ought to examine certain programs with a view to seeing what structural changes are needed. Surely we do not need similar structures at both the federal and provincial levels. I have in mind, for example, research and development programs relating to agriculture. There must be less overlapping of such programs. Is it necessary year by year to increase the size of the federal Department of Agriculture when that bureaucracy must oversee and direct ever decreasing numbers of farmers? Surely that is another example of Professor Parkinson's dictum about the growth of bureaucracy.
I could mention other programs in which there is considerable overlapping at federal and provincial levels, programs to do with insurance, loan and trust companies, corporations and securities. Bill C-16, now before committee, deals with the so-called better protection of this country's depositors and borrowers; yet we are finding in the committee that many of the provisions of that bill are nothing but poorly-worded versions of laws already standing on the statute books of most of our provinces. We are proposing to subject business to these further regulations and costs. Why? Why can we not clear away this underbrush of legislation, do away with this overlapping of jurisdictions and provide Canadians with efficient
February 24, 1977

government? The same point can be made with respect to matters of culture, heritage and sports. Why can we not streamline our methods and avoid duplication and overlapping?
I come now to the question of housing. Surely our high cost of housing stems from the fact that four levels of government, four jurisdictions, are involved in deciding whether a house can be built on a certain lot. Those jurisdictions are the municipal jurisdiction: sometimes, in some areas, the regional jurisdiction, the provincial jurisdiction and, finally, the federal government. The federal government has some say with respect to housing developments which may be under consideration. We must direct our attention to these questions and I am disappointed because there has been so little debate in this House on the important subject I am raising.
I raise another point. This government often pays lip service to the need for greater productivity in industry. But could we not increase our productivity by making the government less non-productive? For example, in the field of industrial development and trade promotion do we need overlapping activities? Do we need, in our international activities, the sort of duplication in consulting, information services and direct lending which now exists? Surely it is worth taking a fresh look at the subject with a view to seeing if we cannot simplify our procedures.
There is considerable overlapping of activities in the field of energy conservation. Actually, the activities of one department of government may run counter to the activities of another. Such lack ot co-ordination is counterproductive. As well, one level of government may do something that from the viewpoint of another level of government is counterproductive. Certainly, the efforts of various levels of government to conserve energy are often counterproductive. In addition, we must streamline our programs of manpower training, unemployment insurance, services to immigrants, communications, research and statistics. I choose those programs since in those areas the federal government could well take the lead in providing more efficient services for the taxpayers we represent.
My second point is this. If we are to create a climate of confidence as between provincial and federal governments, a climate which is essential if there is to be a meaningful restructuring of programs, we must make certain that there is a greater degree of trust between provincial and federal levels of government. Here I raise something which is absolutely shameful. The federal government gave the provincial government of Ontario an undertaking with respect to the purchase of urban transit equipment. The Ontario government, on the strength of that undertaking, went ahead and arranged for the building of that urban transit equipment. Now that provincial government finds that the federal government is reneging on that commitment. That is absolutely unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, I was touching on the government's reneging of its promise with regard to the purchase of certain urban transit equipment. That question, I suggest, merits some further investigation in this House. May I also touch on the extent to which the government's estimates as tabled in this House early last week show evidence of government restraint, or to what extent did the government create the illusion of restraint which is non-existent? To what extent did the government transfer a great bulk of its expenditures to other levels of government? Hon. members will no doubt recall that the former minister of finance, Mr. John Turner, said on June 23, 1975:
The government proposes to set an example of restraint... by imposing strict control over its activities and programs.
With those words, the former minister of finance began a publicity offensive designed to convince Canadians that the federal government was serious about reducing the growth rate of its expenditures and was leading the way in restraint. On Wednesday of last week the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) tabled the main estimates of federal spending for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1978. These estimates were the second set of main estimates tabled since Mr. Turner's statement. The effectiveness of the restraint program since then is best indicated by the fact that proposed federal budgetary spending, as measured by the main estimates, will be $8,934 million greater than at the time of Mr. Turner's statement-an increase of 27.7 per cent in two years. If restraint has been practised, it has not been apparent.
The latest set of main estimates appears to be a model of moderation, in them the government proposes to increase budgetary spending by only 7.1 per cent over the main estimates of fiscal year 1977. But as the figures will show, once again restraint has been more cosmetic than real. Once again, the positive signs of spending moderation are awash in a sea of extravagance.
The greatest single item of what the administration calls restraint has been achieved in the area of grants, contributions and transfer payments. This area of expenditure is forecast to grow by only 1.1 per cent compared to the 1977 main estimates. I point out that it was to these areas of expenditure that ministers formerly appealed when pleading that further restraint was impossible. The record shows, however, that restraint is indeed possible here, for reasons which I shall describe.
As a matter of fact, all transfer payments, subsidies and public debt payments show a considerable moderation in growth. These items formerly deemed uncontrollable, together grew by 3.5 per cent between the main estimates of 1977 and 1978. But where expenditures are more readily controllable, no such moderation is in evidence. The operating and capital expenditures of all departments and agencies are forecast to increase by 14.5 per cent over the same period-a rate more
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
than double that about which the President of the Treasury Board was gloating last Wednesday when he brought these estimates down. When the former minister of finance argued that federal spending controls would be "giving a lead to others in the exercise of restraint", apparently what he meant was that others outside the federal bureaucracy should bear the burden of restraint so that the bureaucracy could maintain the profligate style to which it has become accustomed.
In percentage terms, the planned increase in the number of people employed in the federal public service appears quite small. The number of man-years authorized by the Treasury Board, which excludes military personnel and employees of Crown corporations, will increase by 0.6 per cent from the main estimates for 1977 to 1978. While a marked reduction from the spectacular rates of growth of previous years, a 0.6 per cent increase still means that an additional 2,081 man-years have been authorized for 1978. Further, the rate of increase of planned continuing employees-permanent employees-is 1.1 per cent over the same period, so 3,137 permanent employees will be added in fiscal year 1978.
The discrepancy between the rates of personnel expansion for permanent employees and those for authorized employees reflects a declining proportion of part-time and casual employees as well as a greater ability and willingness of departments to allocate more salary funds to permanent employment. The development is the continuation of an established trend. On a main estimates basis, in fiscal year 1974 the proportion of permanent employees to authorized employees was 90.2 per cent; in fiscal year 1975, 91.6 per cent; in fiscal year 1976, 92.6 per cent; in fiscal year 1977, 93.0 per cent: and in fiscal year 1978 this proportion will rise to 93.4 per cent.
The number of employees involved in this shift to permanent employment can be illustrated by one example. If the fiscal 1978 proportion, 93.4 per cent, were replaced by the fiscal 1974 proportion, 90.2 per cent, 11,238 fewer employees would be allocated to permanent employment. I mention this because when such steps as these are taken by the federal government they generally end up with a counterstep being taken at the provincial government level. Bureaucracy at the federal level begets bureaucracy at the provincial level and the financial implications are significant.
In addition to the fact that greater proportions of authorized man-years are certain to be used up, full-time employees are eligible for the benefits of public service employment, particularly that of an indexed pension. As well, if the federal government ever should decide to make a concerted effort to reduce the size of the public service, it will be much more difficult to lay off permanent employees, who have a sort of tenure, than to simply discontinue the hiring of casuals. Wages and salaries within the public service, excluding Crown corporations, are forecast to rise by 10.7 per cent between the main estimates for 1977 and 1978. Some part of this increase is accounted for by the increased size of the public service, but still on a per-capita basis wages appear to be forecast to rise at a rate greater than that permissible during years two and three of the anti-inflation program-8 per cent down to 6 per cent.
February 24, 1977

It is unlikely that the federal government would be so blatant as to contravene its own AIB guidelines. If the public outcry against excessive federal spending has taught the present administration anything, it has taught it to be subtle and cunning in the ways in which expenditures may be raised. The reason per capita salary increases are likely to exceed 10 per cent may be traced to the continuation of the trend toward a greater proportion of higher echelon employment. While conclusive evidence cannot be supplied until the completion of a comprehensive study of the new estimates, a survey of departments indicates that a greater proportion of executive, professional and senior administrative persons are being appointed than technical, support and operational staff. In other words, the federal public service is becoming more and more top-heavy. The trend has been conclusively established for the period from fiscal year 1974 to fiscal year 1977, and it appears as if it is continued into 1978. Insufficient data is published to reveal the precise financial implications of the shift; however, the general implications of it are clear. Even excluding wage increases and staff increases, the average cost to the public purse of a civil servant is rising.
Another component of the cost of the federal bureaucracy is to be found under the heading "Other personnel costs", and again I draw attention to this because it is bound to provoke a like response at the provincial level. These costs, which include government contributions to pension funds as well as allowances of various kinds, have risen by 14.3 per cent from the main estimates 1977 to 1978. This category of expenditure has grown very quickly over recent years. Whereas government budgetary expenditures grew by 27.7 per cent between the main estimates of 1976 and those for 1978, "other personnel" costs grew by a remarkable 47 per cent. Yet the government dares tell the Canadian public it is showing restraint.
The inability of the present administration to control the size and cost of its bureaucracy is well illustrated, I suggest, by the Figures I have cited. However, one sidelight which sets the tone for this inability may be added. The number of man-years authorized under Treasury Board control has increased by 2,081 between 1977 and 1978. The number of man-years authorized not under Treasury Board control has remained stable, and even decreased.
Another category of federal expenditure where restraint is not in evidence is that of "Purchase, repair and upkeep", the term used in the estimates, which grew by 19.7 per cent between the 1977 and the 1978 main estimates. This category does not include all the repair and upkeep costs of the government. Those which are undertaken by a department directly are accounted for elsewhere; this item only includes repairs and upkeep that is contracted out. Since the present administration began its restraint program, either breakages have been very high or departments have been less willing to perform repairs themselves. From 1976 to 1978 this category of expenditures is expected to increase by 69 per cent. I said repairs and upkeep are contracted out. It will be interesting to see to
Federal- Provincial Fiscal Arrangements what extent they have been contracted out to friends of the Liberal party.
A further example of immoderation in spending is found under the heading of "Utilities, materials and supplies". Money expended under this heading is applied to the more prosaic "necessities" of the bureaucracy ranging from the gas bill and supplies for indigent Indians to mail bags and even paper-clips. While one might have hoped that significant restraint could have been achieved here, expenditures are forecast to grow by 13.9 per cent from the main estimates for 1977 to 1978; and by an amazing 40.1 per cent between 1976 and the upcoming fiscal year.
Other areas of significant increases in government expenditure are those of construction and acquisition of land and buildings-up 10.6 per cent-and machinery and equipment, up 15.6 per cent. Also of note is that the cost of funding the public debt has increased by 15.1 per cent, although this cost would only be controllable by bringing the rest of government expenditures under control. As mentioned previously, controversy over federal spending increases has taught the government to be cunning in the ways spending is increased. Not surprisingly, then, the single greatest spending increase in percentage terms occurs in the category for which there is little accounting: the term is "All other expenditures". All other expenditures include payments to Crown corporations and what the Treasury Board calls "Sundries". From main estimates 1977 to 1978, these expenditures increased by 30.3 per cent; from 1976 to 1978, by 49 per cent.
Crown corporations account for nearly 70 per cent of spending in this category, and spending in these corporations is forecast to average an increase in excess of 35 per cent. Crown corporations are those entities about which minister after minister stands in this House and tells us they will not respond to questions concerning their activities. How often are we told that these corporations have their own boards and that the boards are to be left as laws unto themselves, with no proper supervision by the House or those who are responsible to the House?
Large spending increases in this category are not confined to Crown corporations. Indeed, the very department that stands in the vanguard of the restraint program, the Treasury Board, is guilty of rapidly increasing spending in this area. The "All other expenditures" category of the central administration of the public service program of Treasury Board-meaning "Sundries" at the departmental level-is forecast to increase by an astonishing 978 per cent between main estimates 1977 and 1978.
Turning to areas of expenditure where restraint apparently has taken place, one may note an expenditure increase of 1.5 per cent on information, of 6.5 per cent on rentals and of 8.7 per cent on professional and special services. In these cases, however, it should be noted that restraint is forecast to take place in fiscal year 1978 only after a mammoth spending spree in fiscal year 1977. Since the announcement of the restraint program, taking main estimates 1976 as a base, spending on information has risen by 26.6 per cent; on rentals, by 43.3 per

February 24, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements cent; on professional and special services, by 28.6 per cent. While it may be appropriate to applaud reformation in these categories, the conversion took place from a base of excess rather than normalcy.
I have mentioned that the principal area of expenditure restraint was in the category of grants, contributions and transfer payments. These payments, formerly called "uncontrollable" by the present administration, are forecast to increase by about 1 per cent between main estimates 1977 and 1978. Because expenditures here account for 56 per cent of total federal budgetary outlays, near to zero growth in this category has the effect of halving the over-all budgetary impact of increases in other areas.
Although the former minister of finance, John Turner, argued in his speech on June 23, 1975, that economy measures will prove to be very painful, the present administration has found that the pain of restraint can easily be lessened by good luck, and by transferring the burden of restraint to others the present administration can take the credit for economy measures while achieving very few economies on its own. In short, Mr. Speaker, as we discuss fiscal relationships with the provinces at the federal level it is clear that the federal government has been less than fair to its provincial counterparts.
Payments to other levels of government are forecast to increase by 1.4 per cent from the 1977 to the 1978 main estimates. Proposed changes in the fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial levels, and the transfer of the former shared-cost programs to the provinces, account for much of the reduction in expenditure growth. Transfers to persons, including family allowances, the federal contribution to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and old age security and the income supplement, will increase by 3.6 per cent.
Subsidy payments are forecast to decrease by almost 28 per cent. A reduction in the cost of maintaining the national oil price is the principal contributor to the spending decrease in this category; the reduction results from a higher national oil price. Reduced costs of maintaining the two-price wheat system also assisted in the spending decline. Other transfer payments are forecast to increase by 20.3 per cent, led primarily by spending on job-creation projects, regional economic expansion projects, and foreign aid payments.
Clearly, federal spending restraint is more illusory than real. If Canadians were to follow the example of the federal government in its 1978 main estimates presentation, the message to them would surely run thus, "Spend more and more, but hide it well. Make sure that others pay the bills. Above all, dissemble and deceive".

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE FOR MAKING CERTAIN FISCAL PAYMENTS AND OF ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the question is put, may I just deal with a number of points which have been raised in the debate. Firstly I should like to reply to the point made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), and repeated by a number of other members, that, in effect, the arrangements made between the federal and provincial governments in some way shut out any role parliament may have in this regard.
I certainly recognize that there is a contradiction or conflict between the situation of the House of Commons and the Senate on the one hand which have to enact the bill and the arrangements that had to be made between the two levels of government to provide the substance of it. I am not sure how this can ever be resolved.
One can be quite certain that if the federal government had brought forward these propositions first, not by presenting them to the provinces but presenting them in a debate in the House of Commons, one would have heard from the provinces, objections that they were being called to comment on a set of proposals that had not yet been presented directly to them and upon which they had not had the full opportunity of consultation. Inevitably, the process has to start somewhere. It seems equally inevitable that a federal-provincial agreement of this kind should be preceded, as this was, by extensive consultation, recognizing of course that the House of Commons must ultimately pass judgment on the proposals put forward.
One of the points raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), and repeated by a number of members by that group, is that the transfer of taxation benefits to the provinces as arranged under the established programs financing would provide an actual deprivation for the particular province. I point out that the arrangements here not only provide in favour of the provinces a transfer of taxation room which, of course, will mean a difference in the ability to recover costs from province to province depending on the relative income in each province, but in addition provide for an equalization factor.
Not pnly is the province with a lower income getting the benefit of the tax resource, but the federal government pays a special equalization payment to bring the transfer payment up to the national average levels. In that sense, it is quite true that one of the provinces with a higher range of income, such as Ontario, will have the benefit of growth over time of taxation
February 24, 1977

points. At the same time, the less well-to-do provinces will be protected by this additional form of equalization.
One of the members who spoke this afternoon said that the federal government had approached these discussions on a "take it or leave it" basis. If that had really been our approach, if that had been the formula, we would hardly have spent 18 months in official, finance ministerial and prime ministerial discussion with the provinces. After the meeting of December 13, certain premiers came away from that meeting-Premier Davis was one-saying that it was a tough negotiation and, like every negotiation, they did not get everything they wanted; but on the whole it was a pretty fair deal worked out for the next five years. It was far from being a "take it or leave it" proposition. There was extensive negotiation and extensive adjustment by both parties. It can fairly be said it is a bargain that has been struck between the two levels of government, the agreement arrived at, and not in any sense imposed on the provinces.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), and other members as well, referred to the so-called conditions that will apply with regard to the transfer for post-secondary education and with respect to the existing established programs for medical and hospital care. My colleague, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), dealt with the circumstances surrounding post-secondary education. The fact is, as hon. members know, that the field of education is being jealously guarded by the provinces. There are at stake national interests in education such as the ones referred to by the hon. member, the ability of students to move from province to province without financial impediment and the meeting of certain national goals in education. The provinces have resolutely insisted on making this decision in the absence of any direction and, until recently, any participation by the federal government. We agree with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that it would be desirable to achieve these national goals in education. However, she should recognize that it is difficult to meet these goals when the provinces insist that the federal government should not have a substantial say in certain aspects of the program.
With regard to medical care and hospital care conditions, the famous four points that were in the basic program, we would anticipate that the program is being well established; it really requires no enforcement by the federal government to make sure that the four points are adhered to. The electors of the individual provinces will ensure that the level of hospital and medical services to which they have become accustomed and to which they are entitled will be maintained by the provincial governments.
We have had an extensive discussion not only of this bill, which I concede is a difficult bill, but on a broader basis. I anticipate that myself and my two colleagues will be participating at some length in committee on more detailed questions. Therefore, at this point I will let the debate rest as we move on to the next stage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE'TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, when we were debating this bill and before ten o'clock arrived I had just managed to mention the case of Bill Buchanan, the former chairman of the AntiDumping Tribunal, who was treated by the government in a very shabby way. The record indicates very well the approach the government has taken in the past to the protection of personal privacy.
Perhaps I should recapitulate Mr. Buchanan's history very briefly. He had been chairman of the Anti-Dumping Tribunal. He had done some private work for glass companies when he was in private business. Consequently, he did not sit on the hearing which dealt with the subject of imported glass being dumped in Canada, feeling there might be a conflict of interest. However, following some conflicting legal advice, he joined with the other two members of the tribunal in signing the final judgement when it came out.
Two years later, in 1972, federal tax investigators swooped down on Mr. Buchanan claiming to be carrying out a tax audit, searched his files and took away some documents related to his previous dealings with the Canadian glass companies. It was the former minister of justice, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the person who introduced the last bill which was ostensibly designed to protect individual privacy, who then moved in the courts to overturn the tribunal's decision. He also passed the file to Mr. John Turner, who was then minister of finance, and Mr. Turner demanded Mr. Buchanan's resignation. Mr. Buchanan submitted his resignation. Subsequently the case was taken to the Supreme Court
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).J
February 24, 1977

and the justices unanimously threw the case out. I think it worth while in discussing this case to quote Chief Justice Laskin's ruling. It read, in part, as follows:
I resist the temptation to expatiate on the way in which records were obtained from Buchanan and on the attempted use of the appellants' documents against Buchanan, although obtained on a confidential basis for the purposes of the Combines Investigation Act ... or of the Income Tax Act. 1 say only that unjustified tactics were employed.
I mention this case because it demonstrates graphically the difference between the rhetoric of the government and its performance. It was the minister of finance at the time, Mr. Turner, who made the statement in the glowing phrase which I read into the record when last I spoke on this bill strongly in defence of the principle of protecting human privacy. And it was of course his colleague, the minister of justice, the predecessor of the present minister, with the responsibility for piloting human rights legislation through parliament, who was also responsible for this. Consequently, Canadians have every right to doubt the sincerity of the government.
I have already mentioned that no one really knows how many computerized data banks there are at the federal level. What is clear, however, is that both the number of files about individuals and the amount of information stored in them has grown daily. Let me give the House some examples. In 1974 I put two questions on the order paper asking what sort of computerized data banks there were in existence at that time. Although the information now is dated, I think it is worth while to take a look at some of the answers.
First of all, all government employees have files kept on them, most of which are computerized. Some departments make provision for their employees to see the files; others do not. The Department of National Revenue reported that a record is maintained for each individual required by law to file a T-l return. At the present time records are maintained for approximately 12.8 million employees. There are some 250,000 corporation tax returns, and some 770,000 lists of employers who are making payroll deductions from employees. The Ministry of Transport has a computerized data bank for some
75.000	pilot licence holders.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has a computer data bank of families with children entitled to family allowances, including parents and children up to 19 years of age. There are some 3.5 million families and some seven million children who have personal files in that data bank. There are some 1.8 million recipients of old age pensions and some 1.1 million recipients of the guaranteed income supplement recorded in a computerized data bank. The department also holds files on some 10.3 million contributors to the Canada Pension Plan.
The Department of External Affairs has a new data bank which was established in 1974, which at that time had only
600.000	names, but which was planned to include some 3.5 million people by its fifth year. Also some 30,000 people whose passports are being processed at any one time, and some
20.000	people who are not to be issued passports or whose
Canadian Human Rights
passports have been reported lost or found, are recorded in the data bank.
The Canadian Wheat Board keeps computerized files for some 240,000 producers whose names appear on Wheat Board delivery permits. The names of some 43,000 children of up to one year of age born with birth defects in New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia since 1967 are also recorded, as is the following information; the hospital number and serial number, the name, date of birth, sex, the birth weight, the gestation period, the place of admission or death, the residence code, the place of residence, and types of abnormalities. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, in the past two years many new data banks have been created, and the numbers of people who are on files have grown enormously.
I want to deal briefly with one other file system that the government maintains, and this is the one at the Canadian Police Information Centre, CPIC, which became operational on July 1, 1972. At the present time there are over 850 terminals in Canada. CPIC is also tied into the National Crime Information Centre, NCIC, in Washington, and NCIC has over 40,000 terminals around the United States.
There are a number of different categories of personal information which are listed at CPIC. The most interesting and potentially dangerous ones are in the observation category, described by CPIC as follows: "A person who is suspected of committing an indictable offence but sufficient evidence is not available to prosecute". Note, Mr. Speaker, that these are people who have not been charged with any offence, and all that is needed to open up a computerized file on an individual, which can be kept open indefinitely and made available to police agencies throughout Canada and the United States, with no provision for the person concerned ever to know that he is in the computer, is the claim by an authorized police officer that he suspects that the individual may have been involved in a crime with which he has not been charged.
In that particular computerized file the sort of information that is kept includes a description of the person's activities and a list of people who are seen associating with him. I was concerned when I learned that there were 6,556 people included in this category as of April 20, 1975. However, I had my office check today and learned that in less than two years the Figure has grown by over 50 per cent, and that as of today 10,046 people are listed in this particular category. No one would quarrel with the assertion that our police in Canada deserve the most modern and efficient weapons to Fight crime. But we must also ensure that the rights of our citizens are protected.
What are some of the provisions, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to see included in the right to privacy legislation? First, I should like to see the portions of the bill dealing with privacy severed from the rest of the bill and reintroduced in amended form in the context of an information package dealing both with the question of freedom of information and that of privacy. The guiding principles behind the bill should be that information is the property of the citizens of Canada and not of the government. When the government wishes to coerce

personal information from an individual, or when it wants to deny him information about how public policy is made or about how his money is being spent, the responsibility should be upon the government and not upon the citizen to prove its action is warranted.
Second, the substance of the legislation should be contained within the bill itself, so that parliament knows exactly what it is voting upon. It should not be left to the government to legislate by order in council.
Third, the dangerously broad discretionary powers given any minister to create data banks, whose very existence is secret, simply by exempting them from the provisions of the bill, should be ended.
Fourth, specific provisions outlawing the gathering of certain types of information about individuals, requiring the destruction of files once the purpose for which they were created has ended, providing for an individual's access to his files, and allowing him to challenge the contents of his files, must be included in this bill.
Fifth, there should be an information auditor, similar to the Auditor General, who should be charged with reporting to parliament on how completely departments are complying with the spirit of the act.
Finally, there should be recourse to the courts if an individual feels that he has been unfairly treated. This legislation before us now would allow the government to be judge and jury in its own case.
The development of the computer, like any other advance in technology, brings with it both a promise and a threat. If properly used, the computer will enable us not only to provide services for a growing population more quickly and efficiently, but it will also allow us to build safeguards into the system that will go further toward protecting individual privacy. But, if the government reneges on its responsibility to draw up tough rules for its own conduct, the future of our citizens at the hands of an evergrowing and ever more intrusive government is bleak.
In this bill the government asks parliament and the people of Canada to trust it to regulate itself and not to abuse its enormous power. On the basis of its record, this government has become the most distrusted and disliked in the history of Canada. But even if its record were different and it had proven itself worthy of Canadians' faith, a further question would remain, and that is whether democracy can function on faith alone. In a dictatorship there is little left for the citizens except faith and hope. But in a democracy we know that there should be statutory guarantees to protect the rights of our people.
As a Conservative I know that the interests of the state and the interests of the individual are often in conflict and I know that the bigger government becomes, the smaller each and every citizen becomes. I implore the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to prove that his professed intentions of giving adequate protection to all our citizens are real by allowing the portions of this bill relating to privacy to be substantially

amended at the committee stage. If he will do that, he will have the full support of the members on this side of the House.
But if the government refuses to keep faith with parliament and the Canadian people, one of the first actions of a new government led by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) will be to introduce tough and comprehensive legislation to ensure freedom of information and the right to individual privacy. That is a commitment we make to the Canadian people and, just as this administration will be judged on its record, we are prepared to be judged on ours.

Mr. Speaker, I think both interruptions were unfortunate. 1 would like to continue on the point I was making.
First, this legislation will entrench once and for all, with the teeth of the law, specifically prohibited grounds of discrimination-race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, conviction for which a pardon was subsequently granted, and physical handicap in relation to employment.
Here, I believe, is a large and very significant step forward from the set of ideals that has protected our rights until today, the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Second, I view as evidence of the government's sensitivity to the real needs of the day the categories of prohibited grounds
February 24, 1977

for discrimination included in this legislation which cannot be found in the Canadian Bill of Rights. These are ethnic origin, age, marital status, conviction in the case of a subsequent pardon, and physical handicap in matters related to employment. Nowhere in the Bill of Rights are these considerations mentioned, yet we hear daily of men and women in their fifties who cannot get hired; of the disabled who are considered mentally deficient just because they do not look "normal"; of wives who cannot get work because they are expected to get pregnant instead.
A third innovation which should prove to be a landmark in the history of civil liberties in Canada is the provision for a federal human rights commission. Here, finally, we would have the mechanism required to ensure that our anti-discrimination laws are applied, and applied effectively.
Currently, enforcement of human rights is a highly fragmented process. The provinces each have their own commissions to take care of their areas of jurisdiction, while Part 1 of the Canada Labour Code and a disparate sprinkling of antidiscrimination statutes provide a modicum of protection at the federal level.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, protection of privacy is another area where the government is charting new paths for Canadian society.
On the one hand our citizens will be given the right to see personal information about themselves contained in government records and to correct it if need be. On the other, meanwhile, the government will curtail its own informationgathering activities so that citizens need not be swamped with requests for information irrelevant to their particular case every time they must deal with the government. Moreover, with provision for a privacy commissioner to act as an ombudsman in overseeing the implementation of this aspect of the bill, I believe the Canadian public will be more adequately protected than ever before from invasion of privacy and possible harassment by the government.
I would like to make a few remarks on three special areas- women, the handicapped, and language or linguistic rights. 1 would First like to comment on the subject of women.
To begin with, there is probably no group of individuals in our society more deserving of this legislation than the women of Canada. They have lobbied long and hard for legislation such as this, and it is high time they got it, particularly with reference to their participation in the labour force.
This legislation, when passed, should herald the end of female job ghettoes and unjust pay differentials between men and women. When the effects of this legislation take hold in the labour force, women in managerial positions and the service industries will no longer be earning less than half of what their male counterparts make; women in clerical occupations will no longer have their average earnings exceeded by approximately 50 per cent by men; women in sales occupations will no longer Find themselves earning 150 per cent less than men.
Furthermore, the current trend toward greater participation by women in the upper echelons of government departments
Canadian Human Rights
and the Crown corporations will be strengthened through the encouragement of affirmative action programs, as provided for in this bill.
As hon. members should know, this draft of the bill currently before the House has been revised from the previous human rights bill which died on the order paper last session. Included in this revised version is the concept of equal pay for work of equal value, as opposed to the conventional notion of equal pay for equal or similar work. In the words of the Woman and the Law Association of Ottawa, one of several organizations responsible for inclusion of this principle into the new bill, "it is time women were paid what they are worth".
I can foresee that, in fact, this aspect of the bill may well encounter strong opposition from employers claiming that implementation of such a principle is not practicable. I concede that this could indeed raise problems and that it should be looked into thoroughly when the bill is in committee. In the meantime, however, I would refer those concerned about this problem to a publication prepared by the Department of Manpower and Immigration entitled "The Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupations".
This formula is not perfect, as my colleague, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), has indicated on a previous occasion in this House, but it is certainly a healthy beginning.
Since 1970 the Royal Commission on the Status of Women has been seeking legislative action by the federal government on some 122 recommendations. This bill, incorporating about 30 of those recommendations, would bring our record of implementation up to approximately 103 of 122 proposed by the commission. This record, I believe, indicates the government's serious desire to make up for lost time and provide women with every opportunity to gain an equal footing with men in our society.
The other area I would like to touch on, Mr. Speaker, pertains to protection of the handicapped. As a physician, and one concerned about this country's problems in the field of health care, I am especially pleased to note the extra provision included in this draft of the legislation designed to protect our handicapped citizens from discrimination in the work place.
Like the vast majority of women in Canada, most of our physically handicapped are financial dependants. As they have emphasized repeatedly, however, they do not want, nor do they need, simple handouts from the government or any other source. What they desire is the opportunity to secure a good job and fend for themselves. What has gotten in their way are old-fashioned attitudes and innate prejudice on the part of employers that an individual who does not look "normal" on the outside is necessarily "abnormal" inside as well. On top of this I would suggest that, to date, these people have not been given adequate help in trying to locate jobs which would be suited to their particular talents.
For these reasons, therefore, I believe that the protection extended to handicapped people through this bill should have profound repercussions on how we view these people in the future. Moreover, the sooner we can change employers' atti-

Canadian Human Rights
tude the sooner we shall be able to draw upon the talents and productive capacity of these people as they contribute more fully to the general prosperity of the country.

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out the impact of this bill on the issue that in the eyes of all Canadians is undoubtedly the most important at this time-national unity.
In 1908, on the occasion of the tricentennial of Quebec City, Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated:
"We are proud to say that Canada is the freest country in the world, that all civil and religious liberties are recognized here."
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that such pride is no longer enough today. We can no longer be satisfied with judging the quality of our freedom by comparing ourselves to other countries because there is no doubt that compared to the U.S.S.R., Chile or South Africa we are a free nation but that is not saying much. So we must aim for a higher ideal, an ideal based on our own set of values and reflecting those moral values.
In the Canadian context language rights are a basic element of both individual liberties and national unity. Such rights must therefore be guaranteed and recognized by legislation similar to that which is now before us. In that sense it gives me great pleasure to see that Bill C-25 provides for the creation of a Human Rights Commission which:
(a)	shall develop and conduct information programs to foster public understanding of. .. the principles described-
-in the Act and-
(b)	shall undertake and sponsor research programs relating to its duties and functions-
-under the Act.
I share the opinion that, in most cases, bigotry and racism are caused by ignorance. The act, by allowing us to know one another better, will therefore play a very important role. I cannot stress enough the importance of the task entrusted to the Commission and the need for the latter to be able to count on the full support it needs to fulfill it. In this area we can no longer afford the luxury of failure.
On the other hand, I would also like to stress that the legislation as it now stands does not include language as a prohibited ground of discrimination. If any true significance is to be attached to human rights, as this bill apparently suggests, and if we really want to ensure that every Canadian has a right to deal with the government-

I hope that we will approach some of the problems of national unity which we are facing, in a very tolerant way, otherwise we will have a divided country.
I promised that I would speak for only a few minutes because most of us want to pass the bill tonight and send it to committee to be examined in detail. I might say that all the lead spokesmen of the different parties have praised the main principle of the bill, which I think is a worth-while bill and which all of us welcome. I might say that all the provinces have passed similar bills, and this one is the final bill to give human rights to all Canadians. Therefore, it is a very important bill.
If I were to use a text, I would use the text that eternal vigilance is the price of liberty. From the commencement of time we have seen the trampling and violation of human rights, but in the last generation we have seen serious violations of the liberties of man. I cannot help but think of what happened during World War II and subsequently, and I cannot forget what we in Canada did to the Japanese Canadians. I think it behooves all of us to remember this. In a few months a conference will be held in Belgrade on the Helsinki Agreement. We should keep in mind the trampling and violation of human rights which the people in eastern Europe have suffered, and we should keep in mind some of the terrible discrimination suffered by our black friends in the south. We should also keep in mind the necessity for eternal vigilance because it is the price of liberty.
I hope that this is the first of three steps. When I read the speech of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweath-er) I noted that he said we had the Canadian Bill of Rights but that it was not enshrined in our constitution. It was his hope, as I am sure it is the hope of many of us, that we will reach the stage when we can enshrine the Canadian Bill of Rights in the constitution. There is one other matter that we should remember, that is, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which was passed by the United Nations on December 16, 1948. The main thrust of that Declaration is that all human beings are born free and equal, in dignity, and with rights. We in Canada have not seen fit at this stage to adopt a countrywide declaration of human rights. It seems to me that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the government should give leadership in Canada and move toward the adoption of such a declaration. It should go hand in hand with the
Canadian Human Rights
Canadian Bill of Rights, and it should go hand in hand with the Canadian human rights legislation we are studying at the present time.
I think the main purpose of this bill is to define the prohibited grounds for discrimination, which are race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, physical handicap in relation to employment, or conviction for an offence where a pardon has been granted.
As set forth, the types of discriminatory practices covered in this connection are refusal to employ, a differentiation between persons with regard to promotions, discrimination in advertising of jobs or in questionnaires to be filled out when applying for a job, the exclusion of individuals from membership in employee organizations or segregation of members, refusal to employ the physically handicapped whose handicap does not interfere with performance, and differentiation in wages based on jobs of equal value in the same firm. These are some of the things covered by the legislation, and the setting up of a human rights commission would be for the purpose of enforcing these provisions.
It has been said before, and it should be repeated, that we hope the approach of the commission will be an approach of conciliation rather than prosecution, because in the final analysis conciliation is the proper approach. We cannot legislate freedom; we have to persuade people to be free and to allow freedom for all persons.
I feel that I represent a riding which is a microcosm of the United Nations. The Broadview riding embraces all the races and nationalities of this world. When I moved into the riding in 1948, it was 98 per cent Anglo-Saxon, but as of today it is about 45 per cent Anglo-Saxon, and the rest is made up of the different races and nationalities of the different parts of the world. Hon. members can appreciate the stresses and strains which are imposed on a constituency like Broadview. However, those stresses and strains can be multiplied throughout the city of Toronto and in some of the other, main cities across the dominion.
In recent months we have seen some forms of racism in the city of Toronto. Most Torontonians are not proud of the acts of a small number with regard to the treatment of minorities there. There has been an attempt to reduce the amount of racism in Toronto by trying to bring about a change of attitude in the people who live there. This bill gives some strength and force to the protection of human rights for all persons of all nationalities. Therefore it strikes me as a bill which is very important, and I think all have said that it is important to have as its underlying basis the process of conciliation instead of prosecution.
In a city like Toronto there is not much to be gained by a large number of prosecutions for violations, but I can see a great deal to be gained by the approach of some churches, schools, and social organizations within the communities in an effort to learn the different cultures, languages, and backgrounds of the different people. I am proud to say that within

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate at second reading of Bill C-25, to be known as the Canadian Human Rights Act. All hon. members are aware that this legislation is not new and that it has been around for some time in one form or another. During the last session it was Bill C-72. In spite of that, however, Bill C-25 does represent, as far as I know, an original effort on the part of the government to provide some form of human rights protection at the federal level.
We in this party have no real quarrel with this legislation. Other spokesmen for our party have said earlier that we are prepared to allow the bill to proceed through the House at second reading as quickly as possible, so my remarks will therefore be brief.
The areas of discrimination which this bill will proscribe, and the fundamental human and civil rights which it would protect, are very necessary, worth-while and long overdue measures for enshrinement in a federal statute. Certainly the federal government lags far behind all the provincial governments in the area of civil or human rights legislation.
Part I of this bill would make it an offence to discriminate on most of the usual traditional grounds such as race, ethnic origin, skin colour, sex, and also adds a few innovative ones. Of

course age discrimination is not new, but it is a very common discrimination today against which protection is necessary. Marital status as grounds for discrimination in relation to employment is also something which I am pleased to see included in this bill. Most of us are aware, I am sure, of instances in which a job applicant was discriminated against because he or she was single, or in some cases because he or she was married, or widowed, or divorced.
Also in relation to employment this bill would make it an offence to discriminate on the grounds of a physical handicap. Unfortunately, however, the bill seems to be more concerned here with actual physical disabilities, such as blindness, or paralyzed or amputated limbs, and although epilepsy is specifically included it does not seem that a disease like diabetes, for instance, is included as a grounds for discrimination in employment. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members are aware of the rather celebrated case which occurred up in Pembroke, I think it was, a few months ago, in which a telecommunications clerk was fired because he was a diabetic. Here is an example of discrimination taking place practically on parliament's doorstep. How can we as Canadian parliamentarians defend ourselves against the frequent charge made today that parliament is irrelevant in the modern, contemporary life of this nation, if we cannot address ourselves to a situation like this involving discrimination? The physical handicap clauses of Bill C-25 should be given some more attention in committee.
Making it an offence to discriminate against anyone who was convicted of a crime for which a pardon was later granted is a worth-while protection against a certain type of discrimination. I think, though, that discrimination against convicts who have already served their sentence or otherwise paid the penalty is a far more common type of discrimination against which some protection should be provided in law. Maybe some would say that the percentage of convicts trying to go straight is not very large, but nevertheless this is still discrimination when it occurs. Broadening this part of the bill in this way would seem to be the only logical extension of the type of human rights protection which is envisaged in this particular clause.
I think that the general tone of this bill in the area of proscribed grounds for discrimination is quite progressive on the whole. Perhaps it is too bad that the drafters of the bill could not also have included a few other categories of discrimination such as certain types of unpopular or dissenting political views, as well as religious ones, plus certain types of what are known as alternative lifestyles, that is, interpersonal relationships, and perhaps also sexual orientation, as proscribed grounds for discrimination. These things today are, after all, only in accord with contemporary reality and modern schools of thought or opinions on these subjects. They no longer shock us the way they once did, Mr. Speaker, and extending legislation into these areas does not have the same radicalism about it that it once had. Certainly the only true concept that can underlie any genuine human rights legislation is that social or
February 24, 1977

public discrimination based on one's privately-held beliefs or on one's private life, which is not society's business to begin with, is just as unjust as discrimination based on race or skin colour.
The other provisions of this bill do seem to be real attempts to deal with some contemporary discrimination problems. We have the usual prohibition against discriminatory signs and notices. This would make illegal the notorious "No Englishmen need apply'' type of signs which were common in western Canada a half century ago. Of course discrimination today is much more subtle than this. As well as signs and notices, this bill also deals with the use of the telephone to spread racism and discrimination. The universal and automatic telephone has today become an easy tool for the racist hate mongers, and this bill addresses itself to that problem by making the use of telephones for racist hate campaigns an illegal act, subject to fine or imprisonment.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, proscribing certain practices as discriminatory, and protecting in law certain fundamental human rights, are useless unless the law can be enforced, and for this purpose Bill C-25 provides for a Canadian human rights commission. It is interned that the independence of this commission will be ensured by having the eight members of the commission appointed by order in council and removable only on an address of the House of Commons and the Senate.
1 think it is interesting that the bill does not limit the human rights commission to an enforcing role but also gives it an educational, or what should perhaps more accurately be described as a public relations role. Human rights in Canada would be furthered through public education programs, although it is hard for me to envision how these programs would take place in practice. As part of its public education role the commission could conduct research into discrimination. This is an interesting power to give to the commission. However, it is one which I think could be easily abused. The research would have to be of a hard, practical nature. The nature and scope of prejudice and discrimination have been thoroughly studied by now by various social scientists, and any research which the Canadian human rights commission might do would have to be useful and original and not just chasing after some will-o'-the-wisp.
In addition to this power to undertake research, the commission would also be able to review and comment on federal regulations, rules and orders, to ensure that they are consistent with the principles stated in the bill. This is a very unusual power, with the possible exception of the Anti-Inflation Act, Bill C-73. I think that this is one of the very few times that a bill sets up an internal mechanism for reviewing its own application and enforcement.
It is the latter part of this act, the privacy or protection of personal information provisions of Bill C-25, which our party does not like, Mr. Speaker. These provisions would give an individual access to personal information about himself which is contained in information banks maintained by certain federal government departments or agencies. Bill C-25 in this part makes a weak gesture into the area of freedom of information,
Canadian Human Rights
but that is the best that one can say about it. I know that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) think that this particular aspect of this bill is a tremendous and progressive innovation in Canadian legislation and, given the closeted secrecy which for so long has characterized this government, I suppose that is probably true. But this is not 1940 or 1950, Mr. Speaker. The examples of other countries, particularly the United States and Sweden, show us what can be done in the area of access to government files.
I know that Bill C-25 is not meant to be freedom of information legislation, but the Prime Minister himself suggested at a press conference a few weeks ago that the protection of personal information provisions of this bill might be some sort of substitute for it. This is absurd. It is just another example, similar to the so-called gun control bill of last year, of the government trying to give the impression of doing something about a situation while not really doing anything substantial about it at all. The exemptions attached to this right of access to personal information banks in the federal government are so widespread and comprehensive that in practice this whole part of the bill will be worthless. For instance, 1 see in the schedule attached to this bill that one of the federal government agencies which the individual would presumably have access to is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. However, one of the exemptions provided against access of the individual is, and I quote:
... information or matter . . . obtained . . . in the course of investigations pertaining to the detection or suppression of crime generally.
But by definition a police force's very function is the detection and suppression of crime, and all of the information which it possesses will be obtained through such investigations. In practice this means that nothing in RCMP files will be accessible to anyone. Mr. Speaker, this matter is not just academic, in light of the Prime Minister's statements in this very House only a few days ago that the RCMP probably has files on millions-and those were the words he used-millions of Canadians. This part of Bill C-25 is a good example of how not to approach the whole issue of giving the individual greater access to some government information.
Hon. members are aware that our party has advocated a true freedom of information act for some time. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has spent a great deal of time and effort on this, but his tremendous efforts do not seem to have had any effect on the government. 1 wonder how long the government can go on denying the Canadian public what the citizens of many other democratic states now take for granted. The denial of something which has become such a populist public issue is a position which is, for any government today, almost indefensible. There has not been a time in our recent history during which the public has been so suspicious of government. I am amazed that the present Liberal government, which is already facing such a crisis of confidence among the Canadian people, would adopt such an intransigent attitude with respect to the freedom of information issue.
