subsubtopic: MEASURE'TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in speaking this evening on Bill C-25, the Canadian human rights bill. I think members of all parties support the principle of this bill.
According to archaeologists, human civilizations date back at least 50,000 years. For most of that time the law of civilized societies dealt with commodities, commerce and property. Only recently in human history has the focus of attention shifted to human rights, to a person's feelings which are not part of the external, objective world, but which are most important to every human being.
I am pleased to be a member of the political party which brought forward the Bill of Rights, the cornerstone of our human rights legislation. I say that although my party will vote for the bill, it will by no means end the discussion on human rights in Canada. This bill is only the beginning of the whole debate on human rights which must take place in this country. We have embarked on a new era for human rights, because really for the first time we are passing a law which has to do with a person's feelings, not with trade, commerce, commodity or property rights.
All this being so, is it not ironic that at this very time when the parliament of Canada is debating this human rights legislation, the government refuses to give a strong rebuke to the government of Uganda for its involvement in the death of an archbishop of that country and two Ugandan cabinet ministers, deaths which occurred under conditions of great secrecy and grave doubt? Surely our human rights philosophy must be extended, must be projected to govern our international relations with other countries. In other words, it will not be sufficient to establish fundamental human rights in this country without paying attention to the question of human rights generally in the world.
Historically we have come a long way. We are to enshrine in law the rights of persons. We are passing a law which does not deal with trade, or commercial relations. However, let me point out that passage of this bill will not give us assurance of adequate human rights in Canada. We must recognize that other laws and regulations must be amended if we are to advance significantly our concept of human rights. Perhaps I can give hon. members one or two examples of what I mean.
This human rights bill will not, by itself, assure all of equal opportunities. Why do I say that? At present a farmer is allowed to claim a deduction of $1,830 for his working farm wife. Mr. Speaker, we all know that you cannot hire help on the farm for that sum. But the farmer's wife works on the farm; she may be hauling bales, milking cows, or doing any number of farm chores. Under our tax laws the farmer is not

entitled to claim her as a hired employee-although this difficulty is partly overcome if he incorporates the farm. As matters now stand, the farmer is not entitled to treat his wife as a hired employee for tax purposes; he is entitled to claim a deduction of only $1,830 for his wife who may work full-time on the farm. Such laws must be changed in the name of equity.
Full human rights must be granted to all, and all must be treated fairly. Unfortunately many of our laws treat our native Indians as if they are of second-class status. I am aware of the provisions of the Indian Act and the historical background to that act. Unfortunately, the law abuses our native peoples. The unemployment rate among native peoples is high, as high as 95 per cent on some Indian reserves. At present our national labour force statistics do not include native Indians among the unemployed. Why not, Mr. Speaker? If we are to provide adequate human rights for all our people, we must change many of our laws which presently restrict human rights in Canada. I see no reason for not counting among the unemployed our unemployed native citizens. They should be included in unemployment statistics when those are put forward.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) spoke about the handicapped, and I wish to draw to the attention of the House the existence of regulations which discriminate against certain disabled people. I suggest that such regulations must be corrected if we are to ensure human rights for all. At present those who are blind, confined to a wheel chair, or completely bedridden are allowed a tax deduction of $1,400 a year over and above the normal tax allowance. My quarrel is with the way in which the categories of the incapacitated are defined. The three categories mentioned are entitled to the full tax deduction. Unfortunately other people who are totally incapacitated for health reasons are not included under those provisions of our tax laws.
Last fall when 1 was in British Columbia I met a number of people in Kamloops who were seriously ill. One of them had had a heart attack, another was wearing a metal brace because of a severe back problem. These people wanted a tax deduction equivalent to that available to the blind, bedridden, or those in wheel chairs. Their request was turned down. As a matter of fact I received a letter on this subject just today. Surely those people are entitled to be treated in the same way as those in the first category I mentioned. I am citing these examples to show that we must amend many of our regulations and laws, otherwise some of our citizens will be denied their human rights. As I said, passage of this bill will not, by itself, bring full equity to all Canadians. Unless we change our other laws and regulations, we shall not see full human rights in Canada.
This bill should establish the broad parameters of human rights in Canada. I believe the bill should place a high degree of trust in the courts. Its interpretation will, no doubt, be subject to variation in accordance with our changing Canadian culture.
It would be naive to assume that legislation could ever be written in such a way as to ensure human responses in all
February 24, 1977

circumstances. Perhaps I might give some examples in this regard. It is stated in the bill there is not to be any discrimination on the ground of age. The fact is that, in the absence of opportunities for the courts to make judicial decisions in this regard, discrimination in this sphere will continue to take place. One must certainly question what appears to be happening at the present time-the concept of forced retirement which is so often approved by labour unions as well as by management, business people, and government institutions.
People are considered to be useful and employable at the age of 64, and somehow fit only to be passengers at 65. It seems to me this is not only a tremendous waste of talent and skill but that it is really an affront within the context of this bill. It is an affront to all our human rights because to remain meaningfully involved in our country's affairs is the prerogative, surely, of any citizen. Nevertheless, given the manner in which society is structured at present, the bill before us will not alleviate the situation.
People over 65 who want to work and who have the capacity to work will not be given the opportunity to continue. I am speaking now about the discrimination in respect to age. The bill is not sufficiently specific to be useful in this regard. We read that among citizens over 45 years of age, 37 per cent of the unemployment is long term, while for men of all ages only 27 per cent is long term unemployment. Again, we can turn to the analysis of the data relating to the job retraining program which clearly indicates that citizens over the age of 65 are denied the advantages available to younger people. What we find, then, is personal discrimination in Canada based on age. The bill before us, of itself, fails to take adequate steps in the direction of removing this discrimination.
I should like now to talk for a few moments about the concept of equal pay for equal work, specifically as it is applied to women. The words themselves are, of course, poetic rhetoric. Most women are cast into job ghettoes which are cemented by tradition. The nurse, the telephone operator, the secretary, the bank teller and the waitress can all enjoy equal pay for equal work and still be undervalued. In recent years, according to Statistics Canada, the gap between wages paid to men and wages paid to women for similar work has widened.
The real test should not be "equal pay for equal work'' but rather whether the person who is being paid measures up in terms of skills expected, effort exerted, responsibility demonstrated, and. training or experience required. Conditions of work are a further factor which should be taken into consideration. To take any other view is simply to say that those jobs which have traditionally been reserved for the female part of the population will continue to be so, and that those engaged in them will receive lower salaries and wages than are paid to others employed in work to which different forms of measurement are applied when estimating its value to Canadian society.
I turn now to other aspects of the bill which ought be examined carefully, both here and later in the committee. I refer first of all to Part I, clause 11(1), which states:
Canadian Human Rights
It is a discriminatory practice for an employer to establish or maintain differences in wages between male and female employees employed in the same establishment who are performing work of equal value.
The question is: why is this principle limited only to pay discrimination by sex? Why are the other prohibited grounds of discrimination such as race, religion, and age not included in this clause?
I turn next to another clause of the bill which also needs to be reviewed, in my opinion. I refer to clause 3 in part one which sets out the proscribed grounds of discrimination as follows:
For all purposes of this act, race, national or ethnic origin, colour religion, age, sex, marital status, conviction for which a pardon has been granted, and, in matters related to employment, physical handicap, are prohibited grounds of discrimination.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that this list is much less inclusive than is the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights. That 1948 Declaration was ratified by the federal government in 1976, after provincial consultation and agreement. Article II reads:
Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, religion, language, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.
While we have taken a step forward, the government has failed to go even as far as the United Nations in this regard because the definition 1 have just read in connection with prohibited discrimination suffers from being a closed list in the legal sense that anything not included within it is automatically excluded.
A bill of rights is a bill of principles, not a catalogue of acceptable behaviour. What we really find in the bill placed before us is a catalogue of behaviour rather than an acceptable set of principles subject to a judgment which is left to the courts. The government has sought to anticipate all the possible behaviour of human beings and to determine which kinds of behaviour are acceptable and which are not, without recognizing the fact that it is not possible to predict the changing conditions of our culture. What would be acceptable today might, therefore, not be acceptable at some future time.
The purpose of Part IV of Bill C-25 is to protect the privacy of individuals. While it has been well stated by many members of this party that this part of the bill is one of the most offensive parts to the members on this side, the bill at most gives citizens the right to inspect their files which are held in government information banks. The truth of the matter is that the bill does not define the limits or conditions within or under which the government or any other agency may collect or store information on persons. It is not enough just to be able to inspect individual files in this country; what is more important is that there should be limits placed on the kind of criteria establishing such information banks on individuals.
Far more important than this kind of restriction on the right to inspect files is to impose strict conditions upon the government establishing, either on its own behalf or through any

February 24, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
other private agency, a data bank on human beings in this country. This provision is not made in the bill but 1 hope it can be discussed in committee and amendments made to the bill, so there is not only the right to question the kind of data that are kept on individuals, but so the law itself spells out clearly the limitations placed on the keeping of information on the citizens of Canada. To do otherwise, I think, would be a great affront to Canadian freedoms and human rights.
1 should also like to point out that while the bill provides the right to inspect our files, it does not give us the right to appeal any misjudgment that we believe exists on those files. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said a couple of days ago when he was speaking on this measure, there is no right of appeal provided; the only recourse is to a bureaucratic tribunal, not to the non-partisan judgment of the Canadian courts. So in a case where there is a file kept on a person and the person is not satisfied that the information on the file is accurate or that there should be a file, he does not have full access to the Canadian court system. This kind of biased perspective should not be in a bill that embraces the concept of the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Bill C-25 provides that the privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent consistent with public order and well-being. Compare this modest statement with the wording of the principle enshrined in Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948, which states as follows:
No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his (or her) privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor attacks upon his (or her) honour and reputation. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.
While the government has taken a step forward, it is not as significant a step as we would like to see. To say that we have the right to inspect our files is certainly admirable. But what the bill does not provide is even more important, and that is the setting down of conditions under which any agency in this country can collect data and, file that data away. If we are truly interested in the protection of individual and human rights in this country, that protection would be narrowly defined and cast into the cement of the law. Then agencies would not be able to collect data on people unless they fell within that definition. It is often difficult to find out who has the information, let alone go to the file to see the information for ourselves.
It has been a privilege to speak on this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I want to congratulate the House for having come this far, where we are not only talking about commodity rights, the rights of commerce, trade and property, but also are starting to talk about the rights of human beings. But this bill has not taken the complete step forward. Many changes will need to be made as well to other pieces of legislation. I hope the minister will be amiable enough in committee to make a number of amendments which will tighten up the bill in certain areas, so as to move away from the concept of cataloguing human behaviours. Rather, we should establish the broad principle of the bill and a framework to work within, from which we will develop a proud Canadian act that protects the human rights of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE'TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a pleasure to listen to the speeches made on this bill. As the previous speaker has said, we have come so far as to talk not only about protection of the rights of commerce and other fields of endeavour, but also about human rights. A few years ago the United Nations passed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and we in this country passed an act having to do with a Canadian Bill of Rights. We are now talking about placing a code of rights into our constitution, so it seems to me we have come a long way.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) pointed out very clearly that the bill has many good parts, and that it places in federal legislation provisions that appear in many pieces of provincial legislation. But what the bill does not cover, certainly according to representatives of the Canadian Bar Association, is the protection of personal information and the right to privacy.
It is all very well for lawyers to tell us that we should examine the information on which the government assesses us as individuals, but I am sure most Canadians would ask what business it is of the government to collect such information in the first place. What business has the government to collect information which is not collected to protect the security of the nation? If I were a bank robber and crook-

speechtext: Then you would be a Liberal.

speechtext:
Not necessarily. While I have not engaged in the activities I named, I once did have an RCMP file for some time containing information that I knew about. It also had some information dealing with my small part in a very major strike in the gold mining industry, and some difficulties I had had with the Ontario Supreme Court. There was also information on some small matters, like a little case of assault and battery in which I was involved in some court case. But then the information went on to disclose that I was a rabble rouser, a dangerous character because I had engaged, innocently, as Your Honour would be well aware, in some small disagreement with the government over a veterans' school. The government did not have a very big majority at that time and was very upset about the way that certain discussions had been carried on. There were number of little things like that which were not significant to the security of the nation. However, I have no objection to that being collected because it may lead to something the country should know about. Certain agencies should be established to collect that information.
However, under no circumstances is it important how much money my children receive in family allowances. What business is that of anyone's? The government has to keep an account in order to make a payment. The fact that I receive so much for each child is an accounting detail. Why should that information be put into a computer bank? This is particularly important when you have grandchildren, or possibly great grandchildren. What is the significance of collecting that kind of information? However, that is the kind of information the

February 24, 1977

government collects. In fact it collects a lot of information we do not even know about.
There are now television cameras on Parliament Hill. They scan the area and, if it is desired, pictures are taken of anyone who comes here. These people could be here for peaceful purposes, or for a demonstration. If anyone walks in front of the parliament buildings, the RCMP can take a picture of that person. That can be related to anything else. They then start a file on that individual.
The public are well aware that the bureaucracy is being increased every day. I am sure that to collect these pictures, label them, and identify them will involve dozens and dozens of people. It is done for no specific reason.
Whenever there is a demonstration, the RCMP take pictures. That has always been their little game. Now it is being played in an economic field. It is being played with regard to credit arrangements. We will soon reach the point where it will not be necessary to ask your bank manager whether you can borrow $1,000. All he will do is take your social insurance number, feed that into a computer, and he will know about every debt you have ever owed. He will know whether you owe the income tax people $50 or whether you have a loan with another bank. Some smart kid with a little black box will also be able to get that information on anyone in this country. If it served a purpose, that would be all right. We must be developing a psychotic attitude when those in government believe they need that kind of information. I do not know why they think it will be of any value.
These people must have been watching the movie on television "2001" where big brother in the form of a computer had all the information and knew everything about everybody. I do not see why we need all these computer banks. If the general public knew the extent to which information is collected, they would revolt against it. Do the civil servants require this information because they are going to run this country? The general public would certainly object to that.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) is a learned member of the bar. I understand he had a distinguished career in that field. Therefore, his personal thinking must not be too far removed from the Canadian Bar Association. That association says that if we are to have a well developed country, there must be a disclosure of personal information. If this information is disclosed, I believe that less and less will be collected.
The Bar Association is not my favourite organization. I have no connection with it. My background is that of an underground hard rock miner. Any relationship I had to the law was always on the wrong side of it. However, the Bar Association is violently opposed to this legislation being passed without personal protection. Its members are so violently opposed, they have in effect become apolitical. They have gone so far as to say that, if the minister wishes, they will draft legislation that is in keeping with that of other countries where there is a full disclosure. I suggest the minister consider that offer and bring that before the committee as well.
Canadian Human Rights
I was surprised at some of the explanations given by members of the Bar Association with regard to United States legislation respecting disclosure. The example was given of a person living near an airport. If that person wanted to object to that airport on the basis that there would be too much noise in the vicinity, he could ask the government to disclose to him all documents prepared by the government in relation to the noise surrounding that airport. Then that information could be used by him to prepare a case against the government. The theory is that the information obtained by the government was paid for by individual taxpayers. Therefore all information in the hands of the government should be available to the individual, as well as to the government, in preparing his case.
I was very interested, because normally when lawyers get involved in legislation by regulation they confuse the matter. It usually makes it worse. However, I understood from a representative of the Canadian Bar Association that under United States law you can make an application for disclosure of information which affects you. The agency has ten days to present that information. If it does not present it, it must have good reason. If the information is not made available, the decision can be appealed and the appeal must be heard within ten days. If the appeal is not successful, you can then take the matter before a judge who has another ten days in which to make a decision. I know that is hard to understand because judges do not work very fast.
What happens in the United States is that the matter goes to the top of the docket and it is the first thing the court hears. The judge then receives the document for which the individual is asking. All this is done without lawyers being involved. The judge then looks at the information, considers the arguments that have been made, and decides whether the information is to be made public. If he decides the information is to be made available, it is then released to the individual. If he decides not to release the information, the matter can then be appealed to the highest court. All this must take place within a period of 30 days.
Under that law, it is not necessary to have lawyers on both sides arguing the matter. If the information is to be produced, it is done quickly. For all three stages of the law to be carried out in 30 days is very quick. That disclosure of information means something to the general public and certainly means something to the individual.
I think the minister will be hard pressed to say that the information, whether it is in a computer or in the form of a document concerning the individual, should be disclosed to the individual involved just as it is to the agency, which in this case would be acting as his adversary. But it seems to me that that information should be made available to him. To a layman like me who is not a lawyer it seems only logical that such a disclosure should be made, and there is no reason for not doing so.
I agree that in the case of information affecting national security and also information on criminal activity should be

restricted. But in other cases, why should public servants put a stamp saying "Confidential" on every document they handle, or stamp "To Be Seen By The Minister Only" or some other foolish statement? Are they doing it just to protect themselves against having their work seen and being judged incompetent? In 99 per cent of the cases the document is stamped confidential only to protect the incompetence of the person who produced the report. If that were not so, the author of the document would be proud of producing it and would want it seen.
In other countries people like to see their names on the documents which they prepare. In the United States, for example, many documents are tabled because someone wants his name seen by the public. But in this country everyone is stamping "Confidential" on documents, which are then put away some place where no one can see them, and the only reason for doing so is to hide the incompetence of the person who has prepared them. I am sure it is not the ministers who say that a document should not be released but public servants.
We took a very small step forward when we passed the Canadian Bill of Rights. Many other countries have gone far beyond what the minister is suggesting in the legislation before us, and they have passed their legislation a long time ago. We move very slowly. This legislation has been around for some time. For some reason or other we do not have the proper machinery to update our legislation. The minister has put forward legislation which originally was prepared two or three years ago. Since that time it has not been updated because we do not have the proper mechanism with which to do it.
I hope the minister will agree to accept the offer of the Canadian Bar Association to assist him. I suppose it is the only time in history when they have been prepared to do something for nothing. They are offering to supply the services of some people for free to help the minister. It would be the minister's legislation, but they would be pleased to give him any help he wanted. They were asked what they will get out of it, and they replied, "Nothing. We believe in the rights of the individual, and we want to enshrine in the legislation every possible protection for the individual against the technology that is developing which makes all kinds of information on individuals available to governments and agencies, information about which the individual may know nothing and which he cannot check to ascertain whether or not it is correct". The Canadian Bar Association believes that this is fundamental justice which should be contained in the human rights bill, and that it is absolutely mandatory.
Perhaps I have been misled, and perhaps the minister could indicate some reason why there should be all this secrecy. Perhaps he could go even further and give me a good reason why public servants want to keep so many documents confidential. Let me tell you that in my view there are 20 per cent too many of them, and everybody in the country will agree with that.

There is an interesting comment which I should like to make about this.
This afternoon I was reading about the chairman of the Bell Telephone Company. Apparently when he came to Canada from IT&T his first order to Northern Electric was that they should get rid of their sales people. He said, "We must stop making all the sales we are making and we must get rid of many of our people. We must get down to the point at which we can compete, the point where everyone is hungry and everyone wants to keep his job, and everyone is scared that, if they do not, they will have no job". Perhaps some hon. members know something about Northern Electric, because that is exactly what he did. He trimmed the organization from the top. The managers went first, then he got rid of some of the sales staff. One salesman on the staff was making $1 million worth of sales. Anyone might think that the chairman was crazy, but in the thinking of IT&T if you eliminate a certain percentage from the staff at the top and you increase the efficiency of those who are left, you get a bettter organization. Those who expect an increase in their pay in accordance with their productivity are rewarded.
Everyone will agree that there are many people in the civil service in the top bracket who are just staying in their jobs awaiting their pensions, and who certainly do not want to rock the boat.
The minister knows full well that he has a great opportunity to move forward and not have to follow someone else. He should take the offer of the Canadian Bar Association with regard to the clause relating to the disclosure of personal information. He should accept their kind offer, their generous offer to pay a number of people to provide the government with assistance. We should move forward in this direction as fast as we can.
As my last remark I would like to say that I would be surprised if our country, which believes in the rights of individuals, does not withdraw our ambassador to Uganda. I believe that this legislation would have no teeth unless we agreed to attend the next Commonwealth conference only on condition that Uganda is not invited, because if there has ever been a country going in the opposite direction to what we want to achieve through this legislation it is that country.
If the government really believes in this legislation, then we will withdraw our representative in Uganda, and we will not sit with the representatives of that country at any international conference until their regime is changed. It might even be wise for us to talk to our CIA friends and ask them to put out a contract to eliminate that unsavoury situation so that people in Uganda can again have some rights such as they had under their previous leader, Milton Obote.

I hope, for the sake of himself and his party, that he was being facetious. 1 would not want to call what the hon. member said a joke because it was so silly. 1 trust he was not even trying to make a joke.
1 wish I had time to deal with a number of misunderstandings and misconceptions which arose in this debate about certain provisions and intentions of this bill. Obviously that is something for the committee, when the bill gets there.
The struggle for human rights is an ongoing, ever-present and never-ending one, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said. In this debate we heard discussion of the international scene and, in particular, discussion about Uganda. I am not drawing attention only to the reference just made; references were also made in earlier speeches. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has just returned from Washington where the Helsinki Agreement was discussed. It was on August 1, 1975, that through our Prime Minister our country signed the final act of the Conference on Security and Cooperation at Helsinki, and among the principles with which the 35 governments concerned themselves was the determination to respect and put into practice Principle 7, namely, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief.
In subscribing to these principles each government, including the Canadian government, undertook to promote and encourage the effective exercise of civil, political, economic, social, cultural and other freedoms. I think this bill represents a concrete step, in Canadian legal development, toward giving additional legislative expression to our commitment to the Helsinki Agreement because it extends the existing Canadian human rights laws, both federal and provincial, still further. I
Canadian Human Rights
therefore hope that before the up-coming conference reviewing the Helsinki Agreement we will be able to have this bill passed and become part of the law of the country.
I cannot and will not deal extensively with Parts I, II and III of the bill relating to discrimination. There was much reference in the debate to the Canadian Bill of Rights, and in my introductory remarks I mentioned it myself and paid credit to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). However, some hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), seem to think that we do not need a human rights commission; that we could just legislate, take a legalistic approach, and have all these problems solved in the courts.
I was glad that there were other hon. members, for example, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) who recognized that there must be, in addition to a Bill of Rights, and in addition to a legalistic and judicial approach to this question, a human rights commission which not only has power to investigate, examine and, if need be, impose penalties, but also power to educate and promote or, as the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk) said, engage in P.R. on behalf of the issue of human rights and anti-discrimination. To solve some of these problems we need a commission with the power to conciliate between parties. I am glad that need was recognized by a good number of speakers representing different parties because this aspect has been criticized by some. Undoubtedly that approach should be recommended.
With regard to Part IV of the bill there is immense confusion, it seems to me, about two subjects. One is freedom of information or freedom of access to government documents, and the other is the right of privacy. These are two quite different subjects.
We made it clear in the Speech from the Throne that we would be tabling before the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, through the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), a set of proposals on the first of those subjects, namely, freedom of information or the right to government documents, and to the information upon which the government makes decisions-and this bill does not deal with that issue. Part IV of this bill though deals with the right of individuals to protection of their privacy in terms of government information, the right of an individual, and no others, to see his file and to correct that file. While hon. members can be critical of any proposal, I hope they will make sure they are making that very fundamental distinction, a distinction which is recognized in Sweden and in the United States. There are two things we are talking about, and in Part IV we should be talking about the right of privacy.
With regard to exemptions, every act of this nature has some exemptions. I hope hon. members will examine the exemptions in this bill, not with rhetoric but with care. 1 thought the hon. member for Portage made an excellent speech tonight, but he attacked the exemption for information
8O010-10V2

February 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
used in the course of investigations pertaining to the detection of suspicion of crime. Surely, however, we cannot give drug traffickers the legal right in the course of a drug investigation to apply to the government and obtain the police file on that investigation. If that is to be the case, there will be literally no drug prosecutions or drug convictions in the country. I implore hon. members to look at these exemptions carefully and study them carefully. Obviously it is my job to justify those exemptions in committee. 1 submit that I will be able to do that.
There is much more I would like to say, but I will have to say it in committee. I appreciate the remarks of hon. members. I appreciate the concurrence with my opening statement that I hope we can have the bill passed by June 30. There seems to be general co-operation and support for that proposition. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs is immensely busy right now, and I hope all hon. members will co-operate with that committee to see that we achieve that objective.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CUBA-SUGGESTED RECONSIDERATION OF RELATIONSHIP IN VIEW OF SUPPORT OF RHODESIAN GUERRILLAS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CUBA-SUGGESTED RECONSIDERATION OF RELATIONSHIP IN VIEW OF SUPPORT OF RHODESIAN GUERRILLAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by thanking the parliamentary secretary for making it possible to return to this subject. The department somehow became confused in the returning of answers the last time I raised this question during the adjournment debate, and the parliamentary secretary was good enough to insist to the Clerk and the department that we return to the subject as soon as possible.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), in the closing minutes of the debate on Bill C-25, displayed what I think we could call some mock shock when the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) suggested that perhaps the Canadian government should hire the CIA to investigate the activities of Idi Amin. I do not think I am stretching the point by saying

that perhaps we are doing somewhat the same thing in our relationship with Cuba.
A year ago a question was raised in this House about the use of our facilities at Gander by allowing the Cubans to land planes there. On that point the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) said that we had made it clear we would not tolerate any such use of Canadian facilities for military purposes, if indeed that was the case. A year later we have the shocking declaration that Cuban officials have been using facilities on Canadian soil to train guerrillas to be operatives on the continent of Africa.
Two or three weeks ago newspaper headlines were screaming about the assassination of seven missionaries in Rhodesia. There are allegations and suspicions that the missionaries were assassinated by guerrillas who had been trained by the Cubans. When I posed the question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) two weeks ago he said he thought the question was based on a non sequitur. The very fact that we are giving some form of economic aid to Cuba does not seem to impress the Prime Minister, and it is probably allowing Cubans to carry on furtive activities in other countries in a way they could not if we did not give them the aid. I said in that question that some of the aid is very extensive, and 1 want to put on record some of the figures involved. It strikes me that if we are giving Cuba aid by way of Cl DA almost to the tune of $23 million to $100 million at 3 per cent interest, that is a relatively extensive boost to its foreign aid. I am not speaking of foreign trade but foreign aid. I know there are thousands of people in Canada who would love to have a 3 per cent loan to pay off their mortages. That could be a good war on poverty. Right now the Cubans are waging war, but it certainly is not a war on poverty.
The figures tell us that Cuba has up to 7,000 troops and advisers in the Middle East, 4,000 in Syria, 3,000 in Yemen, and 2,000 in Africa apart from the 12,000 they had in Angola. If we can lend Cuba up to $100 million at 3 per cent interest perhaps that releases some of their other resources for the kind of activities going on in Rhodesia at the present time, so I cannot see why the Prime Minister would say my question was based on a non sequitur. The Canadian people are faced with the dilemma of trying to find out what is the foreign policy of this country. Are we against this kind of activiy being carried on by the Cubans in Africa? If we are, why are we continuing with aid that allows them to carry it on?
The Prime Minister has just come back from Washington saying we ought to be friends with our best friends, who happen to be the Americans in his eyes, at least for the time being. If that is the case, presumably we are thinking of principles of democracy and self-determination, but if at the same time we are allowing the Cubans to carry on guerrilla activities, we cannot be espousing the principles of democracy.
I should like the parliamentary secretary to give us a clear statement of the policy of the Department of External Affairs and of the Prime Minister.Does he in fact espouse democracy as we usually think of it, or does he intend to continue the kind of economic activity with Cuba that will allow them to carry
February 24, 1977

on those activities and let them rape the sanctity of Canadian soil in the process?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CUBA-SUGGESTED RECONSIDERATION OF RELATIONSHIP IN VIEW OF SUPPORT OF RHODESIAN GUERRILLAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall answer the question asked by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) concerning the advisability of reconsidering our relationship with Cuba because of that country's support of Rhodesian guerillas.

The government's position on foreign intervention in Africa, and particularly in Angola and Rhodesia, has been clearly stated on a number of occasions. We are completely opposed to foreign military intervention into these countries. This opposition as it then related to Angola was reiterated on a number of occasions in this House, as well as in a public statement made on January 20, 1976, by the then secretary of state for external affairs, the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen). It was also brought to the attention of Premier Castro by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during his trip to Cuba early last year. This opposition to the introduction of troops and material is still the policy of the government of Canada, and the Cuban government has been made well aware of it.
With regard to our relationship with Cuba, 1 do not think it would be in the best interests of Canada to reconsider it, as it has served us well in the past. It is not our policy to tie the provisions of our development assistance to any given country to the suitability to Canada of that country's foreign policy. We offer our assistance on the understanding that aid will not be used for political purposes but rather for bettering the standard of living of the people of the recipient country. We apply this approach fairly to a number of countries with different political, economic, and social structures. We believe that pursuit of the goal of long-term betterment of the standard of living of the peoples of the developing world is in our best interests, as it is in theirs.
In the case of Cuba we do not believe that the best way to ensure that our advice is followed is by going back on commitments made-or for that matter by tampering with our commercial relationship. Rather, we shall continue to urge them and any others involved to refrain from intervening militarily in the affairs of other nations.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ARSENIC POLLUTION IN YELLOWKNIFE-DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN MINISTER AND HEALTH MINISTER PRIOR TO ESTABLISHMENT OF STUDY GROUP
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ARSENIC POLLUTION IN YELLOWKNIFE-DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN MINISTER AND HEALTH MINISTER PRIOR TO ESTABLISHMENT OF STUDY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have asked both the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) who is looking into the Yellowknife arsenic pollution problem? The Minister of National Health and Welfare said in part, as reported at page 3190 of Hansard,
Adjournment Debate
that the Canadian Public Health Association has been asked to set up a work committee. The minister, in his customary sarcastic manner, suggested that I had failed to understand the nature of the exchange which had taken place between the minister and the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) on the previous day, February 17. I understand exactly what was said.
In his exchange with the Minister of National Health and Welfare the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby referred to the Clean Air Act. On February 18 the Minister of National Health and Welfare was referring to the Environmental Contaminants Act, as is evident if one reads the exchange reported at page 3190 of Hansard. The minister said:
. . . The question of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby dealt with a very specific matter, namely the setting up of standards under the Environmental Contaminants Act.
If the minister had read the question of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, he would have seen that it referred to the Clean Air Act, not to the Environmental Contaminants Act. Nevertheless, the Minister of National Health and Welfare finally admitted after that long exchange with the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby that a joint committee had been set up under the Ministry of the Environment and, one must assume, the Ministry of National Health and Welfare. Its purpose is to consider every aspect of the issue currently confronting the people of Yellowknife.
On the face of it two separate committees have been established, the one established by the Ministry of the Environment and the other by the Ministry of National Health and Welfare, under the auspices of the Canadian Public Health Association. Yesterday, when I asked the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment questions, in an attempt to determine if the Environmental Contaminants Act was being invoked, the minister failed to understand the thrust of my question. Previously, the Minister of Health said I should consult with the Minister of the Environment:-"He knows what I am talking about, ask him when he returns to the House; I am sure you will get this matter clarified."
It was clarified by the Minister of the Environment yesterday when he said to me, "Maybe I did not understand the hon. member's question", and when I put it to him again, he said, "We have a special committee in place under the Canadian Public Health Association".
The point is that parliament passed a bill called the Environmental Contaminants Act, a bill which comprises a schedule of contaminants clearly laid out and which must be investigated by the Department of the Environment. Arsenic is one of the substances listed in that schedule. On reading the bill I find that the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of National Health and Welfare may jointly appoint advisory committees to review any data collected pursuant to the act, more specifically with reference to environmental contaminants. Obviously such a committee is not in place. There appears to be some sort of joint committee which has not been

February 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
defined, though it could have been defined in the response the Minister of the Environment gave yesterday. But this he failed to do. We have that committee, we have a Public Health Commission, and protection under the Environmental Contaminants Act which the minister has failed to implement.
The Environmental Contaminants Act is not a lengthy bill. It is interesting to note that it went into force on March 1, 1976, and that to date no charges have been laid under the statute. I am pleased, of course, that we should have such a clean environment and that everything is moving so smoothly. But when I consider that we also have on the statute books an Ocean Dumping Control Act which was assented to even earlier, an act which really pertains to the same objectives, though in the oceans and inland waterways, 1 become somewhat doubtful since no charges have been laid under that act either.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Ministry of the Environment has totally and completely failed to implement anything in the Environmental Contaminants Act, to exercise any of its rights under that act as well as under the Ocean Dumping Control Act. I suggest that the Minister of the Environment in his response to me yesterday clearly showed that he does not know what is going on in his own department with reference to an act which is of paramount concern to that ministry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ARSENIC POLLUTION IN YELLOWKNIFE-DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN MINISTER AND HEALTH MINISTER PRIOR TO ESTABLISHMENT OF STUDY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) presumably refers to section 3(4) of the Environmental Contaminants Act in which it is stated:
The Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare may jointly appoint advisory committees to review any data collected pursuant to subsection (1) and paragraph (3)(a), to receive representations from interested parties or concerned members of the public and to advise the Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare respecting measures to control the presence in the environment of any substance or class of substances.
The Department of Fisheries and the Environment, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the Department of Indian Affairs have been addressing the Yellowknife arsenic problem for some time under their respective legislation. These considerations have included federal government authority under the Clean Air Act, the Fisheries Act, and the Northern Inland Waters Act. It is doubtful whether establishing an advisory committee at this time under the Environmental Contaminants Act would have contributed anything more to the solution of this problem than is already being done.
It should be emphasized that the focus of the Environmental Contaminants Act is upon the widespread contamination of the environment associated with the commercial use of problem substances. I might add that arsenic is included in the list of priority substances under consideration for major investigation under the Environmental Contaminants Act.
A priority setting exercise has been under way for some time in an attempt to establish short lists of problem substances. The two departments are now reviewing responses from across the country, greater than 100 replies to date. It is planned to distribute a summary of this survey for further comment.
|Mr. Brisco.]
No advisory committees under the Environmental Contaminants Act have been appointed as yet. We have had working groups and task forces to examine the technical issues about such chemicals as PCB's and fluorocarbons. Formal advisory committees may be required to examine in detail the wider issues of acceptable risk and social-economic impact once technical issues are resolved.
With respect to the specific Yellowknife arsenic problem, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) supported the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the appointment of the special Canadian Public Health Association committee to provide an independent appraisal of the risk to human health.

subtopic: MANPOWER-PRACTICE OF SUPPLYING WORKERS TO COMPANIES WHOSE EMPLOYEES ARE ON STRIKE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
MANPOWER-PRACTICE OF SUPPLYING WORKERS TO COMPANIES WHOSE EMPLOYEES ARE ON STRIKE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) told this House that when it came to strikes his department was neutral. He made that comment in response to a question I had raised concerning the fact that the Manpower Department was referring workers to work in legally struck plants, specially at the Ottawa Journal and Wyandotte Chemicals in Scarborough. Manpower has referred unemployed workers to both these plants. Mr. R. Lapointe of the Manpower Department stated in a telegram, in relation to the Wyandotte plant:
Wyandotte Chemicals Limited has had a standing job order for storemen since December 10, 1976. To date 26 referrals have been made by C.M.C. resulting in six placements.
There are two questions involved in this particular issue. One is impartiality, and the minister's answer touched on the question of impartiality. The minister says that what has taken place is all right. He said last Thursday in response to the question I asked in the House, as reported at page 3137 of Hansard:
If an employer, who also pays substantial taxes, wants to make use of Canada Manpower Centres to indicate a job vacancy, we tell the workers that there is a vacancy but that the plant is on strike. If the individual opts not to go he is not penalized.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the workers pay taxes too, and thanks to the way that the government has handled our tax structure, they pay a great deal more in taxes than employers do. But that is not the question I want to raise tonight. What benefits do they get from the minister's department during a strike or lockout? As for the question of impartiality, the very nature of the Unemployment Insurance Act forbids their receiving unemployment insurance during a work stoppage as a result of a labour dispute. The act is very clear in this regard. So they do not get unemployment insurance.
The government claims that if it paid these people unemployment insurance it would be taking sides in the dispute, and no one will argue with that. That is a quite correct position to take. It is not taking sides in the dispute when it funnels people to jobs formally held by other people involved in labour disputes. This is what the minister would have us believe. But I
February 24, 1977

suggest it is taking sides when it allows a Canada Manpower centre to be used as a referral centre for jobs at a legally struck plant.
It seems to me that on the one hand the government says it is not taking sides when it lets the Manpower centre be a referral centre for jobs at a legally struck plant; on the other hand, the government says it is not taking sides when it comes to paying the strikers unemployment insurance. It cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. It cannot have its cake and eat it too. If the government is to be neutral, it has to be completely neutral. The Manpower centre ought not to be used at all by either employer or employee during a legal strike.
The government says that people involved in labour disputes can go to Manpower centres to get temporary work. This at this time in our history is a sick joke. The government knows that there are about one million people out of work in this country today. It knows perfectly well there is a big difference between finding a new job and filling one that is advertised.
The second point is even more serious than the whole question of impartiality. When the government and the Manpower Department allow Manpower centres to be referral centres for jobs at legally struck plants, they pit brother against brother, worker against worker. In this economy there are desperately few jobs being created and a very large number of people are unemployed. It is obvious that people want to work. Manpower makes these jobs in the struck plants public to all people who frequent Manpower centres. In fact men and women looking for jobs will jump at the opportunity, even though it states in the fine print that a legal strike is in process. It is most dehumanizing placing brother against brother, sister against sister, in the scramble for jobs.
The government's practices in this regard are even more evidence that when it comes to a difference between business and labour, the government's neutrality is pretty one-sided.
What does business get out of this? It gets a large pool of unemployed people. The private sector gets a guaranteed supply of scab labour to fill its plants every time there is a strike or lockout. It gets it from a government agency paid for out of the taxes of Canadian workers. Those on strike pay taxes and their taxes go to support a Manpower centre that is participating in an effort to replace them in a legally struck plant.
What do the employees get? Nothing. They cannot get unemployment insurance benefits while the government is sending scabs in to fill their jobs. That would not be neutral. That is why workers at The Journal were denied unemployment insurance. Their jobs were filled by workers referred by the Manpower centre and escorted to their jobs by the police. These workers are on a legal strike. While they are out on the pavement, their jobs are being filled by scab employees referred by the Manpower centre. These people are being denied relocation grants because Manpower says there is a strike in process.
The jobs are not there for the workers, thanks to the government's deliberate attempts to wreck the economy in the
Adjournment Debate
name of fighting inflation. If people doubt that the government works only for business, they will sure have their noses rubbed into that fact if they are ever forced into a strike or lockout situation. This is the situation as it exists.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MANPOWER-PRACTICE OF SUPPLYING WORKERS TO COMPANIES WHOSE EMPLOYEES ARE ON STRIKE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Manpower and Immigration does not participate in any activity aimed at breaking a strike. On the contrary, it tries to keep its neutrality in all labour conflicts.
Nevertheless, the placement services of Canada Manpower Centres are available to all employers and employees affected by a conflict and who want to use them. That is how Manpower Centres register striking employees and present them to other employers. They also receive job opportunities offered by employers who face a labour conflict and try to fill them. However, before offering a job, Manpower Centres inform workers, orally and in writing, that the employer in question is involved in a labour conflict. Once they know this, workers are then free to accept or refuse the offer. That way, employers and workers can both decide whether they will avail themselves of the placement service of the department if a labour conflict arises. By keeping its neutrality, the department tries not to cause any prejudice to either party.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) will certainly understand that although department officials may observe the strictest neutrality in this type of situation, they will always be criticized by both parties involved, each claiming that they are acting against its own best interests. If it offers the employer the workers he needs, the unions will accuse the department of helping management to break the strike. On the other hand, if it does not, both the employer and his organization will accuse it of helping the union stop the operation. Although each of the parties will generally consider the minister is favouring the other, any impartial observer will find that he is really neutral.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission also remains neutral in cases of employer-employee conflicts. Should a recipient refuse to fill a vacancy resulting from such a conflict, he will not be prevented from receiving unemployment insurance benefits, because such a vacancy is not deemed as a normal working opportunity under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Under our collective bargaining system, employers and employees negotiate freely, without governmental interference. The Unemployment Insurance Commission maintains its objectivity by refusing its financial assistance to workers who are unemployed because of a working conflict. I am sure that the hon. member for Nickel Belt will recognize now that the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission are doing their utmost to remain impartial whenever industrial conflicts arise.
